314:
The diagnosis is alcoholic fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) — reversible fatty change due to alcohol. With continued drinking it may progress to alcoholic hepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Explanation

  • Diagnosis: fat droplets in hepatocytes = fatty change/steatosis; alcohol is among the commonest causes of significant fatty liver.
  • Nature: fatty change is a manifestation of reversible cell injury.
  • Future: [Knowledge – Ch 18] stopping alcohol reverses steatosis; continued abuse → alcoholic hepatitis (the Mallory-Denk "alcoholic hyaline" inclusions) → fibrosis → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure, increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
277:
Cellular ageing is the progressive decline in cellular function and viability caused by genetic abnormalities and accumulation of cellular and molecular damage from exogenous influences; it is genetically regulated, not merely cells "running out of steam."

  • Individuals age because their cells age; age is a major independent risk factor for cancer, Alzheimer disease and ischaemic heart disease.
  • Regulated by evolutionarily conserved genes (yeast → worms → mammals).
278:
Cellular ageing results from accumulating DNA damage, replicative senescence (telomere shortening, p16/CDKN2A), defective protein homeostasis, and dysregulated nutrient sensing (IGF-1/mTOR, sirtuins), together with ROS and persistent low-level inflammation.

MechanismDetails
DNA damageExogenous agents and ROS damage nuclear/mitochondrial DNA; some persists and accumulates. Haematopoietic stem cells acquire ~14 new mutations/year. Premature-ageing syndromes: Werner (DNA helicase), Bloom, ataxia-telangiectasia
Replicative senescenceFinite divisions → arrest. Telomere attrition (telomerase present in germ cells, low in stem cells, absent in most somatic cells; reactivated in cancer). CDKN2A/p16 activation controls G1→S progression and promotes senescence
Defective protein homeostasisImpaired chaperones and autophagy–lysosome/ubiquitin–proteasome degradation → misfolded proteins → apoptosis. Rapamycin (mTOR inhibitor) extends lifespan in mice
Dysregulated nutrient sensingCaloric restriction ↑ longevity by ↓ insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR signalling and ↑ sirtuins (NAD-dependent deacetylases)
Other contributorsROS, persistent low-level inflammation, metabolic insults (Fig. 2.35)
Morphologic markerLipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" pigment) accumulation

Anti-ageing interventions are largely experimental; their long-term safety and efficacy in humans are not fully understood.

384:
This is acute inflammation, most probably an acute suppurative infection (cellulitis or abscess of the leg, and acute lymphadenitis with possible abscess in the inguinal region), with pain due to prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P, and swelling due to histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes and other permeability-increasing mediators.

Diagnosis. A painful, red, warm swelling is the combination of the cardinal signs of acute inflammation: dolor, rubor, calor and tumour. In the 15-year-old girl, with a swollen leg, the likely diagnosis is acute pyogenic inflammation (cellulitis or an early abscess) due to bacterial infection, usually staphylococcal or streptococcal, through a break in the skin. In the 10-year-old boy with a 7-day painful inguinal swelling, the likely diagnosis is acute (suppurative) lymphadenitis of the inguinal lymph nodes, secondary to infection in the lower limb, perineum or genitalia, which may progress to abscess; the inflamed nodes are enlarged because of hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and increased numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages, and red streaks of lymphangitis may be visible. An obstructed or strangulated inguinal hernia and acute osteomyelitis would be considered in the differential diagnosis.

Mediators of the signs

  • Pain: prostaglandins (PGE₂ sensitises nerve endings), bradykinin, and substance P, together with distension of tissue by oedema and injury by leukocyte products.
  • Swelling: vasodilation and increased permeability of venules caused by histamine and serotonin, bradykinin, leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄, C3a and C5a, PAF; PGE₂ and PGD₂ potentiate oedema, and TNF and IL-1 and leukocyte products sustain leakage.
385:
The most probable diagnosis is acute appendicitis; histology shows neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria with mucosal ulceration and a fibrinopurulent serosal exudate, and the blood shows neutrophilic leukocytosis with a shift to the left.

Diagnosis. Pain in the right iliac fossa for a day or two, with rebound tenderness (peritoneal irritation) and fever in a child or adolescent, indicates acute appendicitis, the classic example of acute suppurative inflammation. It is usually initiated by luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) with bacterial invasion.

Histological findings. The diagnostic criterion is neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria. In early disease there is mucosal congestion, oedema and neutrophilic exudate in the mucosa and submucosa, with neutrophils in the lumen and mucosal ulceration. In established disease there is a transmural neutrophilic infiltrate, with vascular congestion and a fibrinopurulent exudate on the serosa (acute suppurative appendicitis). Severe cases show abscess formation, haemorrhagic necrosis of the wall and gangrene, with a risk of perforation and peritonitis.

Haematological findings. Neutrophilic leukocytosis (usually 12,000 to 20,000/μL) with a shift to the left (increased immature forms) and toxic granulation; raised ESR and C-reactive protein.
386:
The most probable diagnosis is chronic suppurative osteomyelitis of the tibia, in which a sinus discharges pus from infected necrotic bone (sequestrum) surrounded by a sheath of new bone (involucrum).

Pyogenic osteomyelitis, usually staphylococcal and often haematogenous, begins as acute suppuration in the metaphysis. If untreated or inadequately treated, necrotic bone (sequestrum) forms within the pus; the periosteum lays down new reactive bone around it (involucrum), which appears radiologically as sclerosis; and pus tracks through gaps in the involucrum (cloacae) to the skin as a discharging sinus.

Chronic bacterial infection of bone shows a persistent neutrophilic exudate for months, along with chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages), granulation tissue and fibrosis. The shin (tibia) is a common site. Tuberculous osteomyelitis is a differential diagnosis. Management requires removal of sequestrum and antibiotics, and complications include pathological fracture, secondary amyloidosis and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma in the sinus tract.
387:
The most probable diagnosis is tuberculosis, in the form of a tuberculous (granulomatous) ulcer of the chest wall, because epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells indicate a granulomatous inflammation, of which tuberculosis is the prototype.

The finding of epithelioid cells and Langhans-type giant cells indicates granulomatous inflammation, and tuberculosis should always be excluded as the cause when granulomas are identified. A chronic non-healing ulcer on the chest wall suggests cutaneous tuberculosis (scrofuloderma from underlying rib or lymph node disease, with a cold abscess breaking down through the skin). Confirmation requires acid-fast stain (Ziehl-Neelsen) of the smear, culture, PCR, and histology demonstrating caseating granulomas, together with chest radiography and Mantoux or interferon-gamma release assays. Other causes of granulomatous ulcers (fungal infection, leprosy, sarcoidosis) must be considered.
388:
Chronic inflammation with repair by granulation tissue and fibrosis is occurring because of persistent irritation by betel nut, and the important complications are submucous fibrosis and malignant transformation to oral squamous cell carcinoma.

Fibroblast proliferation with angiogenesis (granulation tissue) is the hallmark of the repair phase accompanying chronic inflammation. Chronic inflammation is characterised by mononuclear cell infiltration, tissue destruction and healing by angiogenesis and fibrosis, and occurs through prolonged exposure to a toxic agent, here betel nut and its additives (areca nut alkaloids, tobacco, lime).

Continued injury and repair lead to excessive collagen deposition (oral submucous fibrosis with trismus), epithelial dysplasia and leukoplakia, and the complication of greatest importance is oral squamous cell carcinoma. Chronic inflammation is also a setting for persistent ulceration. Biopsy is required to exclude dysplasia or carcinoma.
389:
The most probable diagnosis is a keloid, an exuberant scar caused by excessive collagen deposition that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, does not regress, and recurs after excision.

A raised scar at an incision site that recurs after excision indicates keloid rather than hypertrophic scar. Hypertrophic scars contain abundant myofibroblasts and excess collagen but remain within the boundary of the wound and tend to regress over several months; keloids grow beyond the boundary of the wound, do not regress and recur. Keloid formation seems to be an individual predisposition (higher in dark-skinned people), and microscopically shows thick hyalinised collagen bundles in the dermis.

TGF-β-driven fibroblast activity and an imbalance between collagen synthesis and degradation underlie it. Rarely, a recurring exuberant fibroblastic proliferation after incision or trauma may represent a desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis), a benign neoplasm, which also recurs after excision; histology distinguishes them. Treatment is intralesional steroids, pressure or silicone, or excision with adjuvant radiotherapy or steroids.
424:
The most probable diagnosis is pulmonary thromboembolism with pulmonary infarction, caused by a thrombus from deep vein thrombosis of the leg veins that developed because of immobilisation and trauma and embolised to the lung.

Diagnosis. Sudden chest pain, cough and haemoptysis in a patient immobilised in hospital for a femoral fracture indicate pulmonary embolism with infarction. The delay of two weeks favours thromboembolism; fat embolism syndrome would present 1 to 3 days after injury with respiratory distress, neurological signs, thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash.

Cause. The cause is deep vein thrombosis of the deep veins of the leg or pelvis. The trauma and fracture, together with immobilisation and bed rest, provide all three elements of Virchow's triad: endothelial injury and release of procoagulants from injured tissue and surgery (hypercoagulability), and stasis from immobility (loss of the muscle pump). A fragment of the thrombus detaches, travels through the venous system and the right heart and lodges in a branch of the pulmonary artery.

Embolic obstruction of small end-arteriolar branches produces haemorrhage or a wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct, causing pleuritic pain and haemoptysis. Many DVTs are asymptomatic and recognised only after embolisation.
471:
The probable diagnosis is Down syndrome, trisomy 21, and the haematological malignancy he is at risk of is acute leukaemia, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and also acute myeloid leukaemia.

Diagnosis. Intellectual disability, a flat facial profile and stunted growth with a single palmar (simian) crease are characteristic of Down syndrome. It is confirmed by karyotyping, which usually shows 47,XY,+21 (about 95%). A translocation or mosaic karyotype is possible, and the type matters for genetic counseling.

Malignancy. Children with Down syndrome have a 20-fold higher risk of precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a 500-fold higher risk of acute myeloid leukaemia.
472:
The likely diagnosis is Turner syndrome, and the classic karyotype is 45,X.

Turner syndrome results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome and is characterised by hypogonadism in phenotypic females. Turner syndrome is the single most important cause of primary amenorrhoea (about a third of cases). The ovaries are reduced to atrophic fibrous "streak" ovaries, so there is little breast development, infantile genitalia and sparse pubic hair.

Associated features are short stature, neck webbing, a low posterior hairline, a shield-like broad chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, and cardiovascular malformations (preductal coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve).

Karyotype. About 57% have 45,X. About 14% have structural abnormalities of the X, such as the isochromosome 46,X,i(X)(q10), ring X, or deletions of Xp or Xq. About 29% are mosaics, for example 45,X/46,XX.
538:
This is a malignant neoplasm of the neck until proved otherwise. The most likely clinical diagnosis is carcinoma of the thyroid, such as papillary or anaplastic carcinoma, that has invaded the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the differential diagnosis is squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx or hypopharynx with metastasis to a cervical lymph node, or a lymphoma. I would confirm it by FNAC and histology, with laryngoscopy and imaging for the extent.

Reasoning. A hard, relatively fixed mass in a middle-aged man that has progressed over months suggests a malignant neoplasm, since benign lesions are usually soft, slow growing, and movable. Hoarseness of voice indicates involvement of the larynx or of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, producing vocal cord paralysis, and it points to a locally invasive tumour. A thyroid swelling moves with deglutition, whereas a lymph node mass is usually lateral and does not, which helps to separate a thyroid primary from nodal disease.

A history of smoking and alcohol, dysphagia, haemoptysis, a previous history of irradiation to the neck, or a family history of thyroid cancer would help to distinguish the possibilities.

Investigations

  1. Clinical examination: the site, size, consistency, fixity and movement with deglutition of the mass, regional nodes, the thyroid, and the oral cavity and pharynx.
  2. Indirect or fibreoptic laryngoscopy to examine the mobility of the vocal cords and look for a laryngeal or hypopharyngeal primary.
  3. Ultrasonography of the neck with FNAC of the mass, thyroid or lymph node (the first-line test); where FNAC is inconclusive, core needle biopsy or excision biopsy and histopathology, which gives the type and grade.
  4. Immunohistochemistry to determine the origin: thyroglobulin and TTF-1 (thyroid), calcitonin (medullary carcinoma), cytokeratin and p40 (squamous carcinoma), and CD45 with lymphoid markers (lymphoma).
  5. Biochemistry: thyroid function tests, and serum calcitonin and CEA if medullary carcinoma is suspected.
  6. Imaging: CT or MRI of the neck and upper chest for local extent and nodal spread, and chest radiograph or CT to look for pulmonary metastases.
  7. Staging by the TNM system after histologic confirmation.
539:
The probable diagnosis is squamous cell carcinoma of the skin of the leg, possibly arising in a chronic ulcer or scar (Marjolin ulcer). The diagnosis is made by a biopsy from the edge of the lesion for histopathology, with assessment of the regional lymph nodes and of the extent of invasion.

Reasoning. A fungating, ulcerated growth that is fixed to the underlying tissue in an older man indicates a locally invasive malignant tumour, which has penetrated through the skin and into the deeper structures. Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest such malignancy. Predisposing factors are chronic sun exposure, a long-standing ulcer, scar, burn or sinus (as in chronic osteomyelitis, which is in the list of chronic inflammatory conditions that predispose to cancer), radiation, and arsenic exposure.

The differential diagnosis includes basal cell carcinoma (locally invasive but only rarely metastasising, and more common on the face), amelanotic melanoma, a soft tissue sarcoma that has ulcerated, and Kaposi sarcoma.

Diagnosis

  1. History and examination: the duration, previous ulcer or scar, risk factors, the size, edge and base of the lesion, fixity to bone or deep structures, and the inguinal and popliteal lymph nodes.
  2. Biopsy: incisional (wedge) or punch biopsy from the edge of the ulcer, including adjacent normal tissue and avoiding the necrotic centre. Histology shows invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls (well differentiated), and the grade is assigned.
  3. FNAC of enlarged inguinal lymph nodes to detect lymphatic metastasis.
  4. Imaging: radiograph, CT or MRI of the limb to assess invasion of bone and deep tissues, and chest imaging or CT for staging.
  5. Staging by the TNM system, which guides wide local excision with adequate margins, possibly with nodal dissection, or amputation for bone involvement, and radiotherapy.
540:
The probable diagnosis is malignant melanoma of the skin of the foot, with metastasis to the right inguinal lymph nodes. The diagnosis is confirmed by excisional biopsy of the lesion for histology with immunohistochemistry, and FNAC or biopsy of the lymph node, followed by staging.

Reasoning. A recently evolving blackish pigmented lesion in an older person strongly suggests melanoma, a malignant tumour of melanocytes, and the new, enlarged regional lymph nodes in the drainage area of the foot (inguinal) point to lymphatic metastasis. Acral lentiginous melanoma of the sole and foot is not primarily related to sun exposure, and it is the commonest type in Asian and African populations.

The differential diagnosis includes a benign nevus, seborrheic keratosis, pigmented basal cell carcinoma, and a haematoma beneath the nail or skin, and reactive lymphadenopathy from infection of the foot, which may enlarge the nodes without metastasis; this can be settled only by microscopic examination.

Diagnosis

  1. Clinical assessment with the ABCDE criteria (asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variegation, diameter more than 6 mm, evolution), examination of the whole skin, and the draining nodes.
  2. Excisional biopsy with a narrow margin of normal skin, down to the subcutaneous fat, for histology. Incisional or shave biopsy is avoided where possible, because the depth of the tumour needs to be measured. Histology shows atypical melanocytes with pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, mitoses, and pagetoid spread, and gives the Breslow thickness, Clark level, ulceration and mitotic rate, which are the main prognostic factors.
  3. Immunohistochemistry: SOX10, S100, HMB-45 and Melan-A confirm melanocytic origin, which also distinguishes melanoma from carcinoma, lymphoma and sarcoma.
  4. Lymph node: FNAC or core biopsy of the inguinal node to prove metastasis (sentinel node biopsy is used when the nodes are not clinically involved).
  5. Molecular tests: BRAF mutation analysis (present in about 60% of melanomas), since BRAF inhibitors produce striking responses in advanced disease, and, where relevant, KIT and NRAS testing. Melanoma also responds well to immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1).
  6. Staging: CT or PET-CT for metastases, and serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and TNM classification.

Hypertension is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure, defined in Robbins as a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or more or a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or more. In about 90–95% of patients the cause is unknown (essential hypertension), and in the remaining 5–10% it is secondary to renal, adrenal or other identifiable disease. Its major complications are ischaemic heart disease and heart failure, stroke, aortic dissection and renal failure.

Blood pressure is a continuously distributed variable, and the harmful effects of pressure rise progressively with no sharp threshold. Both systolic and diastolic levels carry risk. Individuals with systolic pressures below 120 mm Hg and diastolic pressures below 80 mm Hg are normotensive, and the range of 120–130 mm Hg systolic is borderline. Lower thresholds apply when other risk factors such as diabetes coexist.

Between one-third and one-half of adults in the general population are hypertensive by these criteria, and prevalence and vulnerability to complications rise with age. Because blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by peripheral vascular resistance, sustained hypertension reflects an increase in blood volume (mostly through renal sodium retention), an increase in arteriolar resistance, or both.

Causes

  • Essential (primary) hypertension (90–95%). This is a multifactorial disorder arising from the cumulative effects of many genetic polymorphisms interacting with environmental factors. Family history, twin studies and genome-wide studies (more than 500 variants) support a genetic contribution. Heavy salt intake, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity and stress are the main environmental contributors. A common final pathway is inadequate renal sodium excretion, which expands volume, raises cardiac output and causes peripheral vasoconstriction, so that pressure is "reset" at a higher level to restore sodium balance (resetting of pressure natriuresis). Vasoconstrictive stimuli and structural thickening of the arteriolar wall add to the rise in resistance.
  • Secondary hypertension (5–10%).
  • Renal: renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension, in which reduced afferent arteriolar pressure activates renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone), glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, polycystic kidney disease and other parenchymal renal disease.
  • Endocrine: primary aldosteronism (frequently an aldosterone-secreting adenoma), Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, acromegaly, thyroid disorders, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia or licorice ingestion.
  • Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta and polyarteritis nodosa.
  • Neurologic: raised intracranial pressure.
  • Pregnancy-induced: preeclampsia.
  • Drugs and hormones: oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, tyramine-containing foods with MAO inhibitors.
  • Monogenic disorders: Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutations) and defects of aldosterone metabolism (e.g., aldosterone synthase, 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase defects).

Special clinical form. In up to 5% of hypertensive patients the pressure rises rapidly (systolic above 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 120 mm Hg), producing malignant hypertension with renal failure, retinal haemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilloedema. Untreated, it is fatal within 1–2 years. It is often superimposed on pre-existing "benign" hypertension.

Complications

  1. Vascular: Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis and damages the walls of large and medium arteries. This leads to aortic dissection and to cerebrovascular haemorrhage. In small vessels it produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous pink thickening from plasma protein leakage and increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis, narrowing the lumen) and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin" laminated thickening in severe disease, with fibrinoid deposits and necrosis in malignant hypertension), as well as necrotising arteriolitis, particularly in the kidney.
  2. Heart: Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertensive heart disease), which can lead to diastolic dysfunction, left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation, demand ischaemia, congestive heart failure and sudden death. Hypertension also increases the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60%.
  3. Brain: Cerebral infarcts and intracerebral haemorrhage (stroke), and multi-infarct dementia.
  4. Kidney: Arteriolar nephrosclerosis with glomerular scarring, progressing to renal failure.
  5. Eye: Hypertensive retinopathy.

Hypertension is usually asymptomatic until late in its course. Left untreated, roughly half of patients die of ischaemic heart disease or heart failure and about one-third of stroke, and effective antihypertensive treatment dramatically lowers these outcomes.

Arteriosclerosis is the general term for hardening and thickening of arterial walls with loss of elasticity, and it includes arteriolosclerosis, Mönckeberg medial sclerosis, fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is one specific type, an intimal plaque disease of large and medium arteries made of a lipid core and fibrous cap. Its main complications are plaque rupture with thrombosis and infarction, aneurysm formation, atheroembolism, intraplaque haemorrhage and chronic ischaemia from stenosis.

Complications of atherosclerosis

  1. Stenosis with chronic ischaemia. Slow luminal narrowing (critical stenosis at about 70–75% loss of cross-sectional area in the coronaries) causes stable angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease, intermittent claudication, mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic encephalopathy. Collateral flow can compensate when stenosis develops slowly.
  2. Acute plaque change. Rupture or fissuring, erosion or ulceration, and haemorrhage into the plaque expose thrombogenic material. The resulting thrombosis, often completely occlusive, causes acute myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction or sudden cardiac death. Thin-capped, inflamed, lipid-rich "vulnerable" plaques are most prone to rupture, often when stenosis was previously only mild to moderate.
  3. Intraplaque haemorrhage, which expands the plaque and may precipitate rupture.
  4. Atheroembolism of cholesterol-rich debris, which causes microinfarcts distally (for example in the kidneys and legs).
  5. Aneurysm formation (especially abdominal aortic aneurysm) from pressure and ischaemic atrophy of the media with loss of elastic tissue, with the risk of rupture.
4:
Atherosclerosis is a chronic intimal disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which atheromatous plaques, each with a lipid core and fibrous cap, narrow the lumen and predispose to thrombosis. According to the response-to-injury hypothesis, it begins with endothelial dysfunction, followed by lipid accumulation and oxidation in the intima, monocyte recruitment and foam cell formation, platelet adhesion, smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation, and matrix synthesis, all driven by chronic inflammation.

Pathogenesis. The contemporary view holds that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury, driven by modified lipoproteins, macrophages and T lymphocytes interacting with endothelial cells and SMCs. The sequence is as follows.

  1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction. Early lesions begin at sites of morphologically intact endothelium that show increased permeability, leukocyte adhesion and altered gene expression. The three most important causes are haemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation (toxins from cigarette smoke and hypertriglyceridaemia also contribute). Plaques localise at vessel ostia, branch points and the posterior abdominal aorta because nonlaminar flow turns off atheroprotective genes such as KLF2, whereas laminar flow keeps them on.
  2. Lipoprotein accumulation and oxidation. With chronic hyperlipidaemia, LDL accumulates in the intima and is aggregated and oxidised by free radicals from inflammatory cells. Hyperlipidaemia also impairs endothelial function directly by increasing reactive oxygen species and accelerating the decay of nitric oxide.
  3. Monocyte adhesion and foam cell formation. Monocytes adhere to the activated endothelium, migrate into the intima and become macrophages. These engulf modified LDL through scavenger receptors, which cannot be downregulated, and become lipid-laden foam cells (SMCs can become foam cells by a similar route). Uptake of modified lipid releases growth factors, cytokines and chemokines that sustain a vicious cycle of monocyte recruitment. The early lesion is the fatty streak.
  4. Inflammation. Cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids in macrophages activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, producing IL-1, which activates endothelium and recruits more macrophages and T cells. Activated T cells release interferon-γ, which further activates macrophages, endothelium and SMCs.
  5. Platelet adhesion at sites of injury, with release of PDGF and other factors.
  6. Smooth muscle proliferation and matrix synthesis. SMCs migrate from the media (or arise from circulating precursors), proliferate under the influence of PDGF, FGF and TGF, and synthesise collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. This converts the fatty streak into a mature atheroma with a fibrous cap. Lipid accumulates both within cells and extracellularly, and late calcification follows.

Infection with herpesvirus, cytomegalovirus or Chlamydophila pneumoniae has been linked to atherosclerosis only circumstantially, and a causal role is not established.
5:
An atheroma has four components: cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages and T lymphocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification in late plaques. It typically has a superficial fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. The commonest sites are the lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, then the coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries and the circle of Willis.

Composition. A typical atheroma consists of:

  • A fibrous cap at the luminal surface, made of SMCs and dense collagen, whose thickness and collagen content determine stability.
  • A cellular shoulder region beneath and lateral to the cap, containing macrophages, T lymphocytes and SMCs.
  • A necrotic core deep to the cap, containing lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters, often crystalline and seen as empty clefts after processing), debris of dead cells, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and SMCs), fibrin, organised thrombus in varying degrees and plasma proteins.
  • Neovascularisation at the periphery, and calcification in advanced lesions.

Some plaques ("fibrous plaques") consist almost entirely of SMCs and fibrous tissue and may be heavily calcified.

Sites. In descending order of severity: the lower abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries, the coronary arteries, the popliteal arteries, the internal carotid arteries and the vessels of the circle of Willis. Upper limb vessels are usually spared, as are mesenteric and renal arteries except at their ostia. Plaques favour the ostia of exiting vessels and branch points, where flow is turbulent.

Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall. It may be infectious, from direct microbial invasion, or noninfectious and immune-mediated. Noninfectious forms are classified by the caliber of the vessel mainly involved: large-vessel (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis), medium-vessel (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, thromboangiitis obliterans) and small-vessel vasculitis, which is either immune complex–mediated or ANCA-associated.

Vasculitis can be systemic or confined to a single organ, and its manifestations include constitutional symptoms (fever, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise) together with organ-specific features that depend on the vessels involved. The two basic mechanisms are direct invasion of vessels by infectious agents (e.g., Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Mucor), and noninfectious immune-mediated injury through immune complex deposition, ANCA, anti-endothelial cell antibodies, anti-GBM antibodies or autoreactive T cells. Distinguishing the two is essential, since immunosuppression helps immune forms but harms infectious ones.

Vascular tumours are classified as benign tumours and tumour-like conditions (haemangiomas, lymphangiomas, glomus tumour, vascular ectasias and reactive proliferations such as bacillary angiomatosis), intermediate-grade or borderline tumours (Kaposi sarcoma, haemangioendothelioma), and malignant tumours, chiefly angiosarcoma.

Glomus tumour (glomangioma). Vascular ectasias: nevus flammeus (including port-wine stain), spider telangiectasia, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber). Benign tumours usually form obvious vascular channels lined by a monolayer of normal-looking endothelial cells. Malignant tumours are more solidly cellular with cytologic atypia and poor vessel formation, and their endothelial origin may need immunostaining for CD31 or von Willebrand factor.

The major cardiac diseases are heart failure, congenital heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis, pericardial disease, and cardiac tumours. Congenital heart disease is classified functionally into left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA), right-to-left shunts (tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection) and obstructive lesions (coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, aortic stenosis or atresia).

Major cardiac diseases. Heart disease reduces to six pathophysiologic mechanisms: pump failure, obstruction to flow, regurgitant flow, shunted flow, conduction disorders and rupture of the heart or a major vessel. The clinicopathologic groups are:

  1. Heart failure, which is the common end-point of most chronic heart disease.
  2. Congenital heart disease.
  3. Ischaemic heart disease (angina, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease, sudden cardiac death).
  4. Hypertensive heart disease (systemic, and pulmonary or cor pulmonale).
  5. Valvular heart disease (rheumatic heart disease, calcific aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse, infective and noninfective endocarditis).
  6. Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive) and myocarditis.
  7. Pericardial disease.
  8. Cardiac tumours.

Classification of congenital heart disease. CHD arises from faulty embryogenesis during weeks 3 to 8 and is broadly classified by the haemodynamic consequence into shunts and obstructions. About 1% of live births have a significant cardiovascular malformation, and ventricular septal defect (42%) is the most frequent.

Tetralogy of Fallot has four components: a ventricular septal defect, obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis), an aorta that overrides the VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It is the commonest cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

The first three features arise embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, and the right ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to the pressure overload. The VSD is large, with the aortic valve overriding it, so that both ventricles empty into the aorta. The severity of the right ventricular outflow obstruction determines the clinical picture. With mild stenosis the shunt may remain left-to-right with no cyanosis ("pink tetralogy"), whereas with more severe obstruction right-sided pressures reach or exceed left-sided pressures and a right-to-left shunt produces cyanosis.

The heart is classically boot-shaped because of right ventricular hypertrophy, and a right aortic arch is present in about 25% of cases. The pulmonary stenosis protects the lungs from pressure overload, and right heart failure is rare because the right ventricle is decompressed through the VSD.

Ischaemic heart disease is myocardial ischaemia from an imbalance between myocardial blood supply and demand, caused in more than 90% of cases by obstructive atherosclerosis of the epicardial coronary arteries. It presents as angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease with heart failure, or sudden cardiac death.

IHD comprises a group of related syndromes resulting from myocardial ischaemia. In practice the four clinical presentations are:

  1. Angina pectoris (stable, Prinzmetal variant and unstable), in which ischaemia is transient and insufficient to cause necrosis.
  2. Myocardial infarction (MI), in which prolonged ischaemia causes cardiac necrosis.
  3. Chronic ischaemic heart disease, progressive heart failure from accumulated ischaemic damage.
  4. Sudden cardiac death, usually from a lethal arrhythmia.

Unstable angina, MI and sudden death due to acute plaque change with thrombosis are grouped as the acute coronary syndromes. In addition to coronary atherosclerosis (the dominant cause), ischaemia can result from coronary emboli, vasculitis, or spasm.

The history of exertional chest pain relieved by rest and sublingual nitroglycerin points to stable (typical) angina pectoris due to coronary atherosclerosis. The differentials are unstable angina, Prinzmetal angina and myocardial infarction, and noncardiac causes such as aortic dissection, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, oesophageal reflux and musculoskeletal pain. Myocardial infarction is diagnosed in the laboratory by raised cardiac troponin T or I, supported by CK-MB and the ECG.

Diagnosis. Stable angina is caused by chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis, usually with a lesion obstructing more than 70% of the lumen, so that perfusion is inadequate when demand rises with exertion, emotion or stress. The transient ischaemia (usually less than 15 minutes) does not cause necrosis. The pain is classically a crushing or squeezing substernal sensation that radiates to the left arm or jaw, and it is relieved by rest (which lowers demand) or nitrates (which dilate vessels and improve perfusion). Pain provoked in a reproducible manner and relieved in this way distinguishes it from infarction.

Differential diagnoses

  • Cardiac: unstable angina (pain at rest or crescendo and lasting longer), Prinzmetal angina (rest pain from spasm), acute MI (pain longer than 30 minutes, not relieved by rest or nitrates), acute pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, with a friction rub), aortic dissection (sudden tearing pain radiating to the back), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis.
  • Pulmonary: pulmonary embolism, pleurisy, pneumothorax, pneumonia.
  • Gastrointestinal and others: gastroesophageal reflux or oesophageal spasm, peptic ulcer, biliary colic, costochondritis and other musculoskeletal pain, herpes zoster, anxiety.

Laboratory diagnosis of myocardial infarction. MI is diagnosed by symptoms, the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI) and the detection of myocardial proteins in the blood. The test of choice is serum cardiac troponin T or I, which begins to rise within 2–4 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and stays elevated for 7–10 days. CK-MB, which rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal in 48–72 hours, is useful for detecting early reinfarction.

Myoglobin rises earliest but is nonspecific, and LDH (flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2) is now only of historical interest. Serial measurements are taken to document the rise and fall.

The main complications of MI are arrhythmias (the commonest, and the cause of early sudden death), contractile dysfunction with heart failure and cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation, myocardial rupture, pericarditis, mural thrombosis with embolism, ventricular aneurysm, right ventricular infarction, and progressive heart failure.

Nearly three-quarters of patients have one or more complications, and their likelihood depends on infarct size, location and the fraction of wall thickness involved.

  1. Arrhythmias occur in up to 90% of patients (ventricular premature beats, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, bradyarrhythmias and heart block), are maximal in the first hour, and account for most out-of-hospital deaths.
  2. Left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock. Pump function falls in proportion to the myocardium lost. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of transmural infarcts, usually when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
  3. Myocardial rupture (1–3%), most often 3 to 7 days after infarction when necrotic muscle is softest: free wall rupture causes haemopericardium and tamponade, septal rupture produces an acquired VSD, and papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.
  4. Papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation from ischaemia, later from fibrosis or ventricular dilation.
  5. Pericarditis, a fibrinous or fibrinohaemorrhagic reaction 2–3 days after a transmural infarct, and Dressler syndrome weeks later.
  6. Mural thrombosis with the risk of systemic embolism.
  7. Ventricular aneurysm, a late complication of a large anteroseptal infarct, with thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but no rupture.
  8. Right ventricular infarction accompanying posterior septal or inferior infarcts.
  9. Infarct expansion, ventricular remodeling and progressive heart failure (chronic ischaemic heart disease).

The important cardiac biomarkers are the cardiac-specific troponins T and I (the best markers), CK-MB, myoglobin and, historically, LDH. Acute MI is diagnosed by combining typical symptoms, ECG changes and a rise and fall of troponin above the reference limit.

The laboratory diagnosis rests on measuring proteins that leak from irreversibly injured myocytes after the sarcolemma loses integrity. Cardiac troponin T or I, regulatory proteins of calcium-mediated contraction, rise within 2–4 hours, peak at 24–48 hours and remain elevated for 7–10 days. With reperfusion they peak earlier and higher because of rapid washout. CK-MB rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to baseline by 48–72 hours, so it is useful for detecting reinfarction.

Myoglobin rises within 1–3 hours but is not cardiac-specific. LDH rises at 24–48 hours with a flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2 ratio, peaking at 3–6 days. Low-level troponin elevation ("troponin leak") also occurs in heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and sepsis, and large acute rises occur in myocarditis and myocardial trauma, so the clinical context and serial values matter. Supporting tests are the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI), echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality and coronary angiography.

My probable diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction, since severe chest pain with sweating that is not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin indicates prolonged ischaemia with myocardial necrosis, usually from plaque rupture with coronary thrombosis. I would order an ECG, serial cardiac troponins, CK-MB, echocardiography and coronary angiography, and I would expect ST-segment elevation and a rising troponin.

Diagnosis. The pain is severe, lasts more than 30 minutes, is described as crushing and is accompanied by diaphoresis, and, unlike angina, it is unrelieved by rest or nitrates. This indicates acute MI, probably due to occlusive thrombosis over a disrupted atheromatous plaque (an acute coronary syndrome). Aortic dissection must be excluded, since it also causes severe pain.

Investigations and expected results

  • ECG: ST-segment elevation in the leads overlying the infarct (STEMI) when transmural, with later T-wave inversion and pathologic Q waves. NSTEMI shows ST depression or T-wave changes.
  • Cardiac troponin T or I: raised from 2–4 hours, peaking at 24–48 hours and remaining high for 7–10 days (serial sampling, with a rise and fall).
  • CK-MB: raised at 3–12 hours, peaking at about 24 hours and normalising in 48–72 hours. Myoglobin is raised early.
  • Blood tests: neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised ESR and CRP, possible hyperglycaemia, and a lipid profile.
  • Echocardiography: regional wall-motion abnormality and reduced ejection fraction, and evidence of complications (mitral regurgitation, VSD, effusion, thrombus).
  • Chest radiograph: pulmonary congestion if left ventricular failure; mediastinal widening if dissection is suspected.
  • Coronary angiography: shows the occluding thrombus and underlying atherosclerotic stenosis, and allows reperfusion by angioplasty and stenting.

The goal of management is rapid reperfusion ("time is myocardium"), with antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, beta blockers and nitrates.

The likely diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction, with the transient unconsciousness (syncope) most probably due to an arrhythmia such as ventricular tachycardia, heart block or asystole, or to hypotension from acute pump failure. It is confirmed by a raised cardiac troponin (with CK-MB), along with typical ECG changes.

Severe central chest pain with diaphoresis is the classic presentation of acute MI. Syncope in this setting suggests a complication, the commonest being a ventricular arrhythmia (arrhythmias occur in about 90% of patients and are maximal in the first hour), or conduction block in a posterior (inferior) infarct, or hypotension from extensive myocardial damage with cardiogenic shock. Aortic dissection and massive pulmonary embolism, which can also present with pain and syncope, must be considered.

Laboratory investigations. Serial cardiac troponin T or I is the key test and shows a rise from 2–4 hours, a peak at 24–48 hours and persistence for 7–10 days. CK-MB (rise at 3–12 hours, peak at 24 hours, normal by 48–72 hours) is a supporting test. The ECG will show ST elevation (STEMI), and the findings are supported by raised leukocyte count, ESR and CRP. Echocardiography and angiography are performed to define wall-motion abnormality and coronary occlusion.

Rheumatic fever is an acute, immunologically mediated multisystem inflammatory disease that follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis by 2–3 weeks. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells directed against streptococcal M protein cross-react with host cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry). The diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria: evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.

Aetiopathogenesis. Rheumatic fever (RF) is a hypersensitivity (autoimmune) reaction to group A streptococcal antigens, not an infection of the heart itself. Streptococci are absent from the lesions. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with pericardial, myocardial and valvular antigens. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits Fc-receptor–bearing cells such as neutrophils and macrophages, and T-cell cytokines activate macrophages (for example within Aschoff bodies).

The 2–3 week delay (10 days to 6 weeks) reflects the time needed for the immune response. Only 0.3–3% of infected people develop RF, which points to genetic susceptibility. It mostly affects children aged 5–15 years and is favoured by overcrowding and poverty. The chronic valve deformity is the healing and scarring that follows repeated acute inflammation.

Diagnostic criteria (revised Jones criteria). Evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (a rising or raised ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or recent scarlet fever), plus:

The diagnosis requires two major, or one major and two minor, criteria with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection. These criteria are applied differently in low-risk and high-risk populations. In high-risk populations, such as those with a high background incidence of RF, arthralgia may count as a major criterion and lower thresholds for fever and acute-phase reactants apply.

The mitral valve is the valve most commonly affected; it is involved in virtually all cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease, alone in about two-thirds and together with the aortic valve in another 25%. An Aschoff body is the pathognomonic granulomatous lesion of rheumatic carditis, a focus of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells ("caterpillar cells").

Valve involvement. The mitral valve is virtually always involved in chronic rheumatic heart disease, in isolation in about two-thirds of cases and with the aortic valve in another 25%. The tricuspid valve is infrequently affected and the pulmonary valve rarely. Rheumatic heart disease is virtually the only cause of mitral stenosis, producing "fish-mouth" stenosis with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and thickened, fused tendinous cords.

Aschoff body. The Aschoff body is a distinctive lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, found in the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, in any of the three layers of the heart. It consists of an area of fibrinoid necrosis infiltrated by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and large macrophages with abundant cytoplasm (Anitschkow cells). In longitudinal section the central chromatin of these cells condenses into a slender wavy ribbon ("caterpillar cells"), and in cross-section appears like an "owl-eye." Some Anitschkow cells fuse to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells. Aschoff bodies are rarely seen in chronic rheumatic heart disease because of the long interval since the acute illness.

The complications of rheumatic fever are acute carditis with heart failure, arrhythmias and pericardial effusion (fatal in 1–2%), recurrent attacks, and chronic rheumatic heart disease, whose complications include mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis and right-sided failure.

Acute phase. Rheumatic carditis (pancarditis) can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure, and 1–2% of patients die of fulminant cardiac involvement. Fibrinous pericarditis with friction rub and effusion may occur. The arthritis is self-limited and leaves no deformity, and Sydenham chorea and skin lesions resolve. After the first attack, each streptococcal pharyngitis can precipitate a recurrence, and the valve damage is cumulative.

Chronic rheumatic heart disease (years to decades later). Healing by fibrosis produces leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickened, fused cords, causing mitral stenosis ("fish-mouth") and/or regurgitation and aortic valve disease. Consequent complications are left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation and mural thrombi with systemic thromboembolism (stroke), pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and failure, congestive heart failure, superimposed infective endocarditis, and valve calcification needing surgical repair or replacement.

The probable diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever. The history of a sore throat followed 3 weeks later by fever, migratory joint pain, a rash (erythema marginatum) and a subcutaneous nodule, together with a raised ESR and a raised ASO titre showing preceding streptococcal infection, fulfils the Jones criteria. In the heart there is pancarditis with Aschoff bodies, fibrinous pericarditis, myocarditis and verrucous endocarditis along the lines of closure of the mitral valve.

Diagnosis. The child has major criteria (arthritis, erythema marginatum rash and a subcutaneous nodule, with carditis to be sought) and minor criteria (fever, raised ESR), and the ASO titre of 500 IU/mL documents a preceding group A streptococcal infection. The latent period of about 3 weeks is characteristic of an immune-mediated reaction.

Cardiac changes. During acute rheumatic fever focal inflammatory lesions develop in the heart and the characteristic lesion is the Aschoff body, so that any of the three layers can be involved (pancarditis).

  • Pericarditis: fibrinous or serofibrinous pericarditis ("bread and butter" appearance), with a friction rub, which usually resolves without sequelae.
  • Myocarditis: scattered Aschoff bodies within the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, which may cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure.
  • Endocarditis (valvulitis): inflammation of the left-sided valves, especially the mitral, with fibrinoid necrosis in the cusps or tendinous cords. Small (1–2 mm), warty vegetations called verrucae form along the lines of closure. Subendocardial lesions exacerbated by regurgitant jets cause irregular thickenings in the left atrium called MacCallum plaques.

With repeated attacks, healing leads to chronic rheumatic heart disease: leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of chordae, which produce the "fish-mouth" mitral stenosis.

The vegetative (verrucous) endocardial diseases are rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, and Libman-Sacks endocarditis of lupus.

Infective endocarditis is a microbial infection of the heart valves or mural endocardium that produces vegetations of thrombotic debris and organisms, often with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissue. It is classified clinically into acute and subacute forms. Acute endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, and subacute endocarditis is caused by less virulent organisms, chiefly viridans streptococci, on previously damaged valves.

Infective endocarditis requires a susceptible valve and organisms in the blood. The vegetations are made of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells and colonies of organisms, and they may destroy the valve and extend into adjacent myocardium.

Types.

  • Acute IE: a virulent organism (chiefly Staphylococcus aureus) infects a previously normal valve, with rapid destruction, ring abscess and a stormy course.
  • Subacute IE: a low-virulence organism (chiefly viridans streptococci, 50–60% of native valve cases) infects a previously damaged valve (rheumatic, mitral valve prolapse, calcific stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, congenital defects), with an insidious course over weeks to months.
  • Special settings: prosthetic valve endocarditis (early: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus; late: streptococci), endocarditis in intravenous drug users (S. aureus, usually right-sided), and culture-negative endocarditis (about 10%).

Causative agents. S. aureus is the commonest cause overall. Viridans streptococci predominate in subacute disease. Other agents are enterococci, the HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), gram-negative bacilli and fungi (Candida, Aspergillus), the last two carrying about 50% mortality.

Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, which occurs secondary to cardiac, thoracic or systemic disorders. Important causes are infections (viruses, pyogenic bacteria, tuberculosis), myocardial infarction and Dressler syndrome, uraemia, rheumatic fever, SLE and other immunologic disorders, cardiac surgery, neoplasms and radiation.

Pericarditis is classified by the character of the exudate as serous, fibrinous or serofibrinous, purulent (suppurative), haemorrhagic, and caseous (tuberculous). The causes (Robbins Table 12.13) fall into groups:

  • Infectious: viruses (Coxsackie), pyogenic bacteria (by direct extension from empyema or pneumonia, or from blood), tuberculosis, fungi and parasites.
  • Immunologically mediated: rheumatic fever, SLE, scleroderma, postcardiotomy syndrome, post-MI (Dressler) syndrome and drug hypersensitivity.
  • Miscellaneous: acute myocardial infarction (2–3 days after infarction), uraemia, cardiac surgery, neoplasia (metastasis or direct extension, producing serous or haemorrhagic effusion), trauma and radiation.

Symptoms of fibrinous pericarditis are pleuritic, positional chest pain and fever, with a loud friction rub that is lost if a large effusion separates the layers. Healing may leave adhesions, or scarring leading to constrictive pericarditis, and rapid accumulation of even 200–300 mL of fluid can cause cardiac tamponade.

Generalised lymphadenopathy means enlargement of lymph nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions of the body; the important causes are systemic infections (viral, bacterial, protozoal), lymphoid and haematologic malignancies, autoimmune disorders, drug reactions and storage diseases.

Meaning. Lymphadenopathy is an abnormality in the size (usually more than 1 cm), number or consistency of lymph nodes. It is called generalised when nodes are enlarged in two or more noncontiguous (non-adjacent) groups, in contrast to localised lymphadenopathy, in which a single region that drains a particular area is involved. The distinction is clinically important, since localised enlargement usually reflects a regional infection or tumour drainage, whereas generalised enlargement implies a systemic process.

Mechanisms. Nodes enlarge because of (1) reactive hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and paracortical T-cell zones in response to antigenic stimulation, (2) infiltration by inflammatory cells in lymphadenitis, (3) infiltration by neoplastic lymphoid or metastatic cells, and (4) accumulation of macrophages laden with storage material. In children, systemic viral infections and bacteraemia often produce acute generalised lymphadenopathy.

Important causes

  • Infections: viral—infectious mononucleosis (EBV), cytomegalovirus, HIV (persistent generalised lymphadenopathy), rubella, measles, hepatitis B; bacterial—tuberculosis, secondary syphilis, brucellosis, typhoid, plague; protozoal and others—toxoplasmosis, kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), filariasis, histoplasmosis.
  • Neoplasms: non-Hodgkin lymphomas (especially follicular lymphoma and small lymphocytic lymphoma), Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma; widespread metastases are an uncommon cause.
  • Autoimmune and inflammatory disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, adult Still disease, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, Sjögren syndrome.
  • Drug reactions and serum sickness: phenytoin, allopurinol, carbamazepine, hydralazine, sulfonamides.
  • Others: lipid storage disorders (Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases), hyperthyroidism, Castleman disease, Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease, Rosai–Dorfman disease, amyloidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

In a 60-year-old with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and a very high ESR I think first of lymphoma or a lymphoid leukaemia, then tuberculosis and metastatic carcinoma from the head and neck; I would take a careful history and examine all node groups, do a blood count and smear, chest imaging, and establish the diagnosis by FNAC followed by excision biopsy of an entire node with histology and immunophenotyping.

Interpretation of the case. A markedly raised ESR (100 mm in the first hour) indicates a significant systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process, since the ESR is raised by acute-phase proteins and by immunoglobulins. In an older adult the leading diagnoses are non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma (second incidence peak above 55 years), chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, tuberculous lymphadenitis, and metastatic carcinoma; other possibilities include multiple myeloma, HIV infection, sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease and chronic infection.

Approach

  1. History. Duration and rate of growth; painless or painful; constitutional (B) symptoms—unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss of more than 10%; pruritus; alcohol-induced node pain; contact with tuberculosis, cough, haemoptysis; sore throat, dental infection, dysphagia, hoarseness, nasal obstruction, epistaxis or deafness (nasopharyngeal and head and neck primary); smoking and tobacco chewing; drug history; HIV risk; bone pain.
  2. Examination. Size, number, consistency (hard, rubbery, soft), tenderness, matting, fixity and overlying skin changes of the nodes; examination of all other node groups (axillary, inguinal, supraclavicular, epitrochlear); hepatosplenomegaly; careful examination of the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx and larynx, thyroid, breasts and skin; chest and abdominal examination.
  3. Initial investigations. Complete blood count with peripheral smear (lymphocytosis with smudge cells in CLL, anaemia, leukoerythroblastic picture, blasts); ESR and CRP; liver and renal function tests, serum LDH, uric acid, calcium; serum protein electrophoresis; HIV serology; Mantoux test or interferon-gamma release assay; chest radiograph (mediastinal widening, hilar adenopathy, parenchymal tuberculosis); ultrasound of the neck and abdomen.
  4. Tissue diagnosis. FNAC is a useful first step (caseating granuloma with acid-fast bacilli on ZN stain, metastatic carcinoma, or a monomorphic lymphoid population), but it is usually inadequate for diagnosing and subtyping lymphoma because architecture is lost. Excision biopsy of an entire, intact node (not a core or a node from an area of previous scarring) is the investigation of choice, with histology, immunohistochemistry (CD15, CD30, PAX5, CD20, CD3, CD5, CD23, cyclin D1, BCL2, BCL6, Ki-67), flow cytometry, and cytogenetic or molecular studies as required.
  5. Staging and further work-up if lymphoma is found. CT or PET-CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.
  6. If metastatic carcinoma is suggested. ENT examination with endoscopy and biopsy, thyroid assessment, chest imaging, and further evaluation for a primary.

The WHO classification recognises five subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted, which are grouped as classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, which is a distinct non-classic type.

The first four subtypes share a distinctive Reed-Sternberg cell immunophenotype (CD15⁺, CD30⁺, weakly PAX5⁺, usually negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers and CD45) and are lumped together as classic Hodgkin lymphoma. In the fifth, lymphocyte predominant type, the neoplastic cells have a B-cell immunophenotype that differs from the classic type; in the International Consensus Classification this entity has been renamed nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma, dropping the Hodgkin designation.

23:
The Reed-Sternberg cell is the neoplastic giant cell of Hodgkin lymphoma, derived from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell; the classical cell is a large binucleate or multilobed cell with abundant cytoplasm and large, inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli, giving an "owl-eye" appearance.

Definition and origin. The Reed-Sternberg (R-S) cell is the neoplastic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma and is essential for its diagnosis. Single-cell molecular studies show clonal IGH gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation, establishing origin from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. Nevertheless, the R-S cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express most B-cell–specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes.

They constitute only a minority of cells (the tumour is more than 90% reactive lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and plasma cells), recruited by cytokines and chemokines secreted by the R-S cells.

Morphology of the classical (diagnostic) R-S cell. A large cell, 45 µm or more in diameter, with abundant, slightly basophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm. The nucleus is bilobed or multilobed—classically two mirror-image nuclei or lobes lying side by side—each with a thin, sharply defined nuclear membrane, vesicular, open (clear) chromatin, and a large, inclusion-like, eosinophilic or amphophilic nucleolus, about the size of a small lymphocyte (5 to 7 µm), surrounded by a clear halo, giving the "owl-eye" appearance.

Variants

  1. Mononuclear (Hodgkin) variant: a single nucleus with a large inclusion-like nucleolus.
  2. Lacunar cell: a cell with a delicate, folded or multilobated nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm that retracts during fixation, leaving the cell in an empty space (lacuna); characteristic of nodular sclerosis.
  3. Lymphohistiocytic (L&H, "popcorn") variant: polypoid, multilobed nucleus with inconspicuous nucleoli, fine chromatin and moderately abundant cytoplasm; characteristic of nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
  4. Mummified cell: a shrunken, pyknotic cell with condensed eosinophilic cytoplasm, the result of a peculiar form of cell death in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
  5. Pleomorphic or anaplastic variants: bizarre cells in lymphocyte-depleted (reticular) Hodgkin lymphoma.

Immunophenotype. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma the R-S cells are CD15⁺, CD30⁺ and weakly PAX5⁺, and negative for CD45 and for most B and T-cell markers; in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma the L&H cells are CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD45⁺ and negative for CD15 and CD30.

R-S–like cells may be seen in infectious mononucleosis, solid tumours and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so diagnosis depends on identifying R-S cells in the appropriate inflammatory background with a confirmatory immunophenotype.

Lymphomas are divided into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and the non-Hodgkin group is subdivided according to the cell of origin into B-cell, T-cell and NK-cell lymphomas, many of which are further classified as indolent or aggressive.

1. Hodgkin lymphoma: classic (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted) and nodular lymphocyte predominant.

2. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms):

  • Precursor B-cell neoplasms: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
  • Peripheral (mature) B-cell neoplasms: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma; splenic and nodal marginal zone lymphoma, extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma; mantle cell lymphoma; follicular lymphoma; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; Burkitt lymphoma; lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; hairy cell leukaemia; plasma cell neoplasms.
  • Precursor T-cell neoplasms: T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
  • Peripheral T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia; large granular lymphocytic leukaemia; mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome; peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified; anaplastic large-cell lymphoma; nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (angioimmunoblastic); enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma; subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma; hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma; adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma; extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma; NK-cell leukaemia.

3. Clinical grouping by behaviour. Indolent (follicular lymphoma, CLL/SLL, marginal zone lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, mycosis fungoides); moderately aggressive (mantle cell lymphoma); aggressive (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphomas, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma); highly aggressive (Burkitt lymphoma, lymphoblastic lymphoma). The most common NHL is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, followed by follicular lymphoma; 85–90% of lymphoid neoplasms are of B-cell origin.
637:
The most probable diagnosis is multiple myeloma, and I would confirm it with serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to show a monoclonal protein, a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing clonal plasma cells, and tests for the CRAB features—calcium, creatinine, haemoglobin—and skeletal imaging.

Diagnosis. The age (peak 65 to 70 years), bone and back pain, punched-out lytic lesions of the skull (1 to 4 cm, sharply demarcated), pathologic vertebral fracture and markedly raised ESR (from rouleaux formation due to the M protein) are characteristic of multiple myeloma. The lesions are destructive plasma cell tumours resulting from increased osteoclast activity (MIP-1α) and inhibition of osteoblasts (Wnt inhibitors), and involve the axial skeleton in decreasing order of frequency: vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis and femur.

How to establish the diagnosis

  1. Blood: haemoglobin (normocytic normochromic anaemia), blood film with rouleaux, ESR, serum calcium (hypercalcaemia), urea and creatinine (renal impairment), uric acid, albumin, β₂-microglobulin, LDH; alkaline phosphatase is typically normal.
  2. Serum protein electrophoresis (a sharp M spike, usually IgG or IgA), immunofixation to type the immunoglobulin, quantitative immunoglobulins (reduced normal immunoglobulins), and serum free light chain assay with κ/λ ratio.
  3. Urine: 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for Bence Jones protein (the dipstick may be negative).
  4. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: increased plasma cells (typically above 30%; 10% or more clonal plasma cells with a myeloma-defining event for diagnosis), atypical and multinucleate forms, flame cells, Mott cells, with CD138⁺, CD56⁺ and light-chain restriction.
  5. Imaging: skeletal survey, or MRI/low-dose CT/PET-CT; MRI of the spine for cord compression if neurologic signs.
  6. Cytogenetics/FISH for prognosis: t(4;14), del(17p), t(11;14), del(13q).

Diagnostic criteria. Clonal plasma cells in the marrow plus CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia, bone lesions) or other myeloma-defining events. Distinguish from MGUS (M protein below 3 g/dL, no end-organ damage), smoldering myeloma and solitary plasmacytoma, and from metastatic carcinoma (lytic bone lesions but no M protein).
638:
This is most probably chronic myeloid leukaemia in the chronic phase, and I would confirm it by peripheral smear, marrow examination and demonstration of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR::ABL1 fusion gene.

Reasoning. A middle-aged adult (peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decades) with a very high white cell count, well above 100,000/µL, and massive splenomegaly from extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, is the typical presentation of CML. The onset is insidious, with fatigue, weight loss, anorexia and a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant, and occasionally acute pain from splenic infarction.

Confirmation

  1. Peripheral smear: neutrophils, bands, metamyelocytes and myelocytes (the full spectrum of granulocytic maturation), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts below 10%; platelets often increased; mild anaemia.
  2. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score: low or absent.
  3. Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia, increased megakaryocytes (small, hypolobated), sea-blue histiocytes.
  4. Cytogenetic and molecular tests: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11), or BCR::ABL1 by FISH or RT-PCR.
  5. Other: uric acid, LDH, vitamin B₁₂ raised; blasts and basophils to define phase.

Differential diagnosis. Leukaemoid reaction (high LAP, toxic changes, no basophilia, no massive splenomegaly, Ph negative); primary myelofibrosis (leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells, fibrotic marrow, lower WBC); chronic neutrophilic leukaemia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (lymphocytes), hairy cell leukaemia (pancytopenia), and the other BCR::ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.

Management note. With a count of 250,000/µL there is a risk of leukostasis and tumour lysis; hydration, allopurinol and cytoreduction are needed, and BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors induce sustained haematologic remission in over 90% of patients and reduce the risk of progression to blast crisis.
639:
This is most likely acute leukaemia—acute lymphoblastic leukaemia being the commonest in a child—and the peripheral blood film would show anaemia, thrombocytopenia and circulating blasts.

Clinical diagnosis. The combination of weakness (anaemia), fever (neutropenia with infection, or the disease itself), joint and bone pain (marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration by leukaemic cells) and gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia) in a child suggests acute leukaemia: the stormy onset over days to weeks, the marrow failure triad and the bone pain are characteristic.

ALL is the most common cancer of children and is more likely (peak at about 3 years, with a second adolescent peak for T-ALL), but AML can present identically; prominent gum hypertrophy and bleeding would suggest AML with monocytic differentiation. Other features sought are lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, testicular enlargement, mediastinal mass and CNS signs.

Expected peripheral blood findings

  • Normocytic normochromic anaemia, with a low reticulocyte count.
  • Thrombocytopenia, often severe.
  • White cell count variable: raised in most, but normal or low in some; neutropenia.
  • Blasts in the smear: in ALL, lymphoblasts of high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, condensed finely stippled chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm; in AML, myeloblasts with delicate chromatin, prominent nucleoli, fine granules and Auer rods.
  • Hiatus leukaemicus (blasts and mature cells without intermediate stages); smudge cells may be present.

Confirmation. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showing 20% or more blasts; cytochemistry (MPO negative and PAS positive in ALL); flow cytometry (TdT, CD19, CD10, CD3); cytogenetics; CSF examination.

Differential diagnosis. Aplastic anaemia (no blasts, hypocellular marrow); idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (isolated thrombocytopenia); juvenile idiopathic arthritis and rheumatic fever (joint pain, but normal blood counts and no marrow failure); infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytes); scurvy (gum bleeding and bone pain).
755:
The probable diagnosis is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as a complication of an obstetric event, because after delivery or an induced (especially septic) abortion, release of procoagulants and endothelial injury trigger systemic coagulation with a bleeding diathesis; it is established by thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT, PTT and thrombin time, low fibrinogen and raised D-dimers.

DIC is most associated with obstetric complications, malignancy, sepsis and major trauma. In obstetric conditions, procoagulants derived from the placenta, a dead retained foetus or amniotic fluid enter the circulation (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, retained products, pre-eclampsia, septic abortion with endotoxaemia). The onset can be fulminant, and acute DIC of this type is dominated by a bleeding diathesis: oozing from the uterus, venepuncture and wound sites, haematuria and petechiae, with shock, oliguria or acute renal failure, dyspnoea, and neurological changes.
