Cirrhosis is a diffuse, irreversible-in-its-established-form process of the liver in which fibrosis and the conversion of normal liver architecture into regenerative parenchymal nodules, surrounded by fibrous bands, is accompanied by vascular remodeling and shunting. It is classified by morphology into micronodular, macronodular, and mixed types, and by aetiology.

Definition. Cirrhosis is a diffuse remodeling of the entire liver into parenchymal nodules (often regenerative) surrounded by fibrous bands, with a variable degree of vascular (often portosystemic) shunting. It is the end stage of many chronic liver diseases. The three hallmarks are diffuse involvement, bridging fibrous septa, and regenerative nodules, with disruption of the lobular architecture.

It is not a specific diagnosis, and cirrhosis and liver failure are not synonymous: some cirrhotic patients, such as those whose hepatitis B is suppressed or whose hepatitis C is cured, may never progress to end-stage disease.

Types

  1. Morphological classification (by nodule size):
    • Micronodular cirrhosis: nodules uniformly less than 3 mm; typical of alcohol-associated cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis), haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction, and hepatic venous outflow obstruction.
    • Macronodular cirrhosis: nodules larger than 3 mm (up to several centimetres), typical of post-necrotic or post-viral hepatitis cirrhosis, Wilson disease, and α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.
    • Mixed (micro-macronodular) cirrhosis.
  2. Aetiological classification: alcoholic, post-viral (post-necrotic), biliary (primary and secondary), cardiac (congestive), metabolic and inherited (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), steatohepatitic (MASH), autoimmune, drug-induced, and cryptogenic (more than 90% of "cryptogenic" cirrhosis is probably burned-out MASH).
  3. Functional classification: compensated and decompensated cirrhosis.
69:
The leading causes of cirrhosis worldwide are chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, with biliary diseases, autoimmune hepatitis, and inherited metabolic disorders as other causes.

  1. Chronic viral hepatitis: hepatitis B (with or without D) and hepatitis C.
  2. Alcohol-associated liver disease (micronodular, Laennec).
  3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), the commonest cause in many Western countries, accounting for most "cryptogenic" cirrhosis.
  4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (secondary biliary cirrhosis), biliary atresia, and cystic fibrosis.
  5. Autoimmune hepatitis.
  6. Inherited and metabolic disorders: hereditary haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, glycogen storage diseases.
  7. Vascular causes: chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Budd–Chiari syndrome), chronic right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis).
  8. Drugs and toxins: methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid, and others.
  9. Chronic parasitic disease: schistosomiasis (periportal fibrosis).
  10. Cryptogenic cirrhosis: no cause identified.
70:
The likely diagnosis is decompensated cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension, most probably alcohol-associated. Gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy reflect hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism from impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogen, and the liver function tests that are altered are bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, globulins, and prothrombin time.

Diagnosis. A middle-aged man with jaundice (hepatic failure), gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy (impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, leading to hyperoestrogenaemia, and hypogonadism), and ascites (portal hypertension with hypoalbuminaemia) has cirrhosis of the liver in a decompensated stage. Other expected findings are palmar erythema, spider angiomas, loss of body hair, caput medusae, splenomegaly, variceal haemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy.

The commonest cause in such a patient is alcohol, and chronic hepatitis B or C and MASH must be considered. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography, elastography, endoscopy for varices, and liver biopsy where indicated, and by testing for the cause.

Liver function tests altered

  • Serum bilirubin raised (mixed hyperbilirubinaemia).
  • AST and ALT mildly to moderately raised (AST > ALT, ratio 2:1 or more in alcoholic cirrhosis).
  • Alkaline phosphatase (and GGT) variably raised.
  • Serum albumin reduced, with raised globulins (reversed A:G ratio).
  • Prothrombin time prolonged (reduced synthesis of clotting factors).
  • Others: raised serum ammonia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism).

Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid in the peritoneal cavity. It is a transudate in most hepatic and cardiac causes and an exudate in infective or malignant causes, and the commonest cause overall is cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension.

Definition. Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, clinically detectable when at least about 500 mL has accumulated (shifting dullness, fluid thrill). In 85% of cases it is caused by cirrhosis. Cirrhotic ascites is serous with a low protein content (less than 3 g/dL) and a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more; the fluid may contain scant mesothelial cells and mononuclear cells, neutrophils suggest infection, and red cells suggest disseminated intra-abdominal cancer.

The overwhelming majority of gallbladder carcinomas are adenocarcinomas, usually arising in the fundus on a background of chronic cholecystitis with gallstones.

Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the commonest malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. The tumours are mainly adenocarcinomas, growing either as a firm, poorly circumscribed mass or as a diffuse infiltration of the gallbladder wall that simulates chronic cholecystitis; they are most often found in the fundus. Microscopically they consist of glands (of intestinal, biliary, or papillary pattern, and occasionally mucinous or signet-ring) in a desmoplastic stroma; in some, cytologic atypia and stromal response are minimal and perineural and vascular invasion help to establish the diagnosis. Rarely, other primary tumours occur, such as neuroendocrine tumours, squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and sarcomas.

The precursor lesions are flat dysplasia (carcinoma in situ), intracholecystic papillary-tubular neoplasms, and intestinal metaplasia. Gallstones are present in 95% of cases, with chronic inflammation the common thread; other risk factors are female sex (at least twice as common), porcelain gallbladder and hyalinising cholecystitis, chronic Salmonella typhi carriage, anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, and, in high-incidence areas (Chile, Bolivia, northern India, and Native American populations), ethnicity. Molecular changes include TP53 mutations and alterations of the EGFR family (HER2) and RAS.

The tumour is diagnosed late (preoperative diagnosis in under 20%), spreading by direct extension into the liver and adjacent organs, along the peritoneum and biliary tree, and by metastasis to the liver and portahepatic nodes; the 5-year survival is less than 10%, but incidental carcinoma found early at cholecystectomy can be cured by resection.

Nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation, characterised by haematuria with red cell casts, oliguria with azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension, whereas nephrotic syndrome is due to increased glomerular permeability and is characterised by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Microscopically, nephritic syndrome shows red cells and red cell casts in the urine and hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli, while nephrotic syndrome shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts in the urine and normal or only thickened glomeruli with podocyte foot process effacement. Serum complement is usually low in nephritic syndrome of the postinfectious type and normal in the common causes of nephrotic syndrome.

Complete explanation

Nephritic syndrome results from proliferative, inflammatory glomerular disease. The cellular proliferation and leukocyte infiltration injure the capillary wall, allowing blood into the urine, and reduce GFR, leading to oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention and hypertension. The classic example is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; others are rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy and proliferative lupus nephritis.

Nephrotic syndrome results from a derangement of the glomerular filter, structural or charge-related, that permits plasma proteins to leak; there is typically little inflammation.

In acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis the serum C3 is low (with normal C4) because the alternative pathway is activated and complement consumed, and it returns to normal in about 2 months. Low complement is also found in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, C3 glomerulopathy and lupus nephritis. In minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy and FSGS — the common causes of nephrotic syndrome — complement levels are normal. Glomerulonephritis is a group of diseases, mostly immunologically mediated, in which the glomeruli are the primary site of injury, usually with proliferation of glomerular cells and an inflammatory reaction. The five main primary glomerular diseases are acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy complete the list.

Complete explanation

Glomerulonephritis denotes inflammatory disease of the glomerulus, most often caused by immunologic mechanisms: deposition or in situ formation of immune complexes, antibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane, or cell-mediated immunity. Because some of the glomerular diseases have no cellular inflammatory component (minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, for example), the term glomerulopathy is used for them.

Diseases in which the kidney is the sole or predominant organ affected are called primary; those that are a manifestation of systemic disease, such as lupus, diabetes, amyloidosis or vasculitis, are secondary.

The primary glomerular diseases are:

  1. Acute postinfectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome
  2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of function
  3. Membranous nephropathy — nephrotic syndrome
  4. Minimal change disease — nephrotic syndrome, the commonest cause in children
  5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — nephrotic syndrome and progressive disease
  6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and C3 glomerulopathies — mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture
  7. IgA nephropathy — recurrent haematuria, the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide
79:
Nephritic syndrome is the clinical presentation of inflammatory glomerular disease, with haematuria and red cell casts, oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension. Its complications include acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia and uraemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema, progression to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and eventually chronic kidney disease.

Complete explanation

The syndrome arises when proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli injures the capillary walls and reduces the glomerular filtration rate. Because of reduced filtration, salt and water are retained and nitrogenous waste accumulates; hypertension arises from the volume expansion and from renin release by the ischaemic kidneys.

Complications in the acute phase follow directly from these disturbances:

  • Acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria, azotaemia and uraemia, accompanied by hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy, with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
  • Circulatory overload, with acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema.
  • Heavy proteinuria, occasionally reaching nephrotic range.

Complications in the later course

  • Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, with extensive crescent formation and rapid loss of renal function over weeks. This is the most serious sequel and may follow postinfectious glomerulonephritis in a small minority of children and more often in adults.
  • Chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease, which may end in end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. Persistent proteinuria and an abnormal GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis.
78:
Acute glomerulonephritis is an acute nephritic syndrome caused by inflammatory proliferation of glomerular cells, of which acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the prototype. It is an immune complex disease: after a pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A β-haemolytic streptococcus, streptococcal antigen, notably pyogenic exotoxin B, and its antibody form immune complexes in the glomerular capillary wall, activate complement, attract neutrophils and monocytes, and cause proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, reducing the glomerular filtration rate.

Complete explanation

Definition. Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a clinical syndrome of acute onset with haematuria, oliguria, azotaemia, mild proteinuria, hypertension and periorbital oedema, caused by diffuse proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli. In its classic form it appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection, mainly in children aged 6 to 10 years.

Role of streptococcal infection in pathogenesis

  1. Nephritogenic strains. Only particular strains of group A β-haemolytic streptococci cause nephritis; over 90% of cases are linked to M types 1, 4 and 12, which are typed by their cell wall M protein.
  2. Antigen–antibody complexes. Streptococcal antigen, most importantly streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B, is first planted in subendothelial sites in the capillary wall, where it forms immune complexes in situ with antibody. The complexes then dissociate, cross the basement membrane and re-form on the subepithelial side, appearing as humps; circulating complexes may contribute.
  3. Latent period. The interval of 1 to 4 weeks matches the time required for antibody production and immune complex formation.
  4. Complement activation and inflammation. The complexes activate complement; C5a and other mediators attract neutrophils and monocytes, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, producing hypercellular glomeruli that obliterate the capillary lumens.
  5. Functional result. GFR falls, causing oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention, oedema and hypertension; damage to the capillary wall allows haematuria and mild proteinuria.

Evidence of an immunological basis. The latent period, elevated antistreptococcal antibody titers, low serum C3 from complement consumption, and granular immunofluorescent deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli, with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, all point to an immune complex mechanism.
80:
The clinical diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The urine is expected to show red blood cells, many of them dysmorphic, together with red cell casts, along with mild proteinuria, white cells, and granular and hyaline casts.

Complete explanation

The age of the child, the periorbital oedema, the high-coloured (smoky) scanty urine and the history of a sore throat about two weeks earlier fit acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period corresponds to the time needed for antibodies to form against nephritogenic streptococcal antigens and for immune complexes to deposit in the glomeruli, causing inflammation. Oliguria and oedema reflect the reduced glomerular filtration rate and salt and water retention, and the coloured urine reflects haematuria.

Expected microscopic urine findings

  • Numerous red cells, many dysmorphic (acanthocytes), reflecting passage through damaged glomerular capillaries.
  • Red cell casts, indicating glomerular origin of the bleeding.
  • Granular and hyaline casts, a few white cells and tubular epithelial cells.
  • Mild to moderate proteinuria (usually less than 1 g/day) on chemical testing.

Supporting tests are a raised antistreptolysin O titer, a low serum C3, and a raised serum urea and creatinine.
83:
Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis, most often due to ascending bacterial infection from the lower urinary tract. It is predisposed to by urinary tract obstruction and stasis, vesicoureteral reflux, instrumentation or catheterisation, pregnancy, female sex, diabetes mellitus, preexisting renal lesions, and immunosuppression.

Complete explanation

Pyelonephritis is one of the commonest diseases of the kidney. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation, usually bacterial, associated with urinary tract infection; chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring involving the calyces and pelvis, which results from recurrent episodes of infection in the presence of predisposing factors such as reflux and obstruction.

More than 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, above all Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. The kidney is reached either by the ascending route from the bladder (the commoner route) or by the bloodstream (as in infective endocarditis or in debilitated or obstructed patients).

Predisposing factors

  • Urinary tract obstruction and stasis, whether congenital or acquired (stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, neurogenic bladder), because residual urine allows bacteria to multiply unhindered.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux, which carry infected bladder urine into the renal pelvis and parenchyma.
  • Instrumentation of the urinary tract, particularly catheterisation, and cystoscopy.
  • Pregnancy, in which 4% to 6% of women develop bacteriuria and 20% to 40% of these develop symptomatic infection if untreated.
  • Sex and age: infections are much more frequent in females up to about 40 years of age; in older males the incidence rises because of prostatic enlargement and instrumentation; congenital anomalies are important in infant boys.
  • Diabetes mellitus, through increased susceptibility to infection, neurogenic bladder and frequent instrumentation.
  • Immunosuppression and immunodeficiency, and preexisting renal lesions with scarring and obstruction.
84:
Urinary tract infection is infection of any part of the urinary tract by microorganisms, usually bacteria, shown by significant bacteriuria and pyuria; it may involve the bladder (cystitis) or the kidney (pyelonephritis). It is most common in females, because of the short urethra and other anatomical and hormonal factors, and also in infants with congenital anomalies, elderly men with prostatic enlargement, pregnant women, diabetics, and patients with obstruction, stones, catheters or immunosuppression.

Complete explanation

Urinary tract infection (UTI) is characterised by bacteriuria and pyuria, the presence of bacteria and leukocytes in the urine. It may be symptomatic or asymptomatic and may involve the lower tract (urethritis, cystitis, prostatitis) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis). By convention a count of 10⁵ or more organisms per mL in a properly collected midstream sample is taken as significant. Over 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, most commonly E. coli.

Who is commonly affected, and why

  • Females. After the first year of life and up to about 40 years of age, infection is much commoner in women. The reasons are the shorter female urethra, the close proximity of the urethral meatus to the anus and vagina, the absence of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid, hormonal changes that affect bacterial adherence to the mucosa, and urethral trauma during sexual intercourse.
  • Pregnant women, because of ureteric dilatation and stasis, with a risk of progression of asymptomatic bacteriuria to pyelonephritis.
  • Infants and young boys with congenital anomalies, such as obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux.
  • Older men, in whom prostatic hypertrophy causes obstruction and incomplete emptying, and in whom instrumentation is frequent.
  • Diabetics, who have increased susceptibility to infection and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
  • Patients with obstruction, stones, neurogenic bladder, catheters or instrumentation, and those who are immunosuppressed.
86:
The probable diagnosis is acute urinary tract infection, most likely acute cystitis with ascending involvement of the kidney, that is acute pyelonephritis, since fever accompanies the dysuria. It is investigated by urine routine examination and microscopy, midstream urine culture and sensitivity, a complete blood count, serum creatinine, and imaging of the urinary tract.

Complete explanation

Dysuria and difficulty with micturition indicate irritation of the bladder and urethra (cystitis and urethritis) in a young woman, in whom the shorter urethra predisposes to ascending infection by enteric bacteria, chiefly E. coli. Fever of five days' duration suggests spread to the upper tract and acute pyelonephritis, which is also suggested if there is loin pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

Investigations

  1. Urine examination. The urine contains many leukocytes (pyuria) and bacteria; microscopy may show leukocyte casts, which indicate renal involvement because casts form only in the tubules. A dipstick may show a positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite test, and there may be microscopic haematuria.
  2. Urine culture and sensitivity on a clean-catch midstream specimen, the definitive diagnostic test, showing significant growth (10⁵ or more organisms/mL) of the causative organism and guiding antibiotic therapy.
  3. Blood tests: complete blood count (neutrophil leukocytosis), ESR/CRP, serum urea and creatinine; blood culture if there is high fever or suspected septicaemia.

The four common types of renal calculi are calcium stones (calcium oxalate with or without calcium phosphate), the commonest at about 70%; struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones, formed after infection by urea-splitting bacteria; uric acid stones; and cystine stones. A single common diagnostic test is a plain X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, which shows radiopaque stones.

Complete explanation

Urolithiasis affects 5% to 10% of people during their lifetime, more often males, with peak onset between 20 and 30 years. The most important determinant of stone formation is a raised urinary concentration of the stone constituents that exceeds their solubility (supersaturation); low urine volume, altered urinary pH, infection, and deficiency of crystal inhibitors (citrate, pyrophosphate, osteopontin, nephrocalcin) contribute.

  1. Calcium stones (about 70%) — calcium oxalate or calcium oxalate mixed with calcium phosphate. Most are associated with hypercalciuria, with or without hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, bone disease), and some with hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria or hypocitraturia. They are radiopaque.
  2. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones (5–10%) — formed in alkaline urine after infection with urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus; they can grow into large staghorn calculi that cast the pelvicalyceal system.
  3. Uric acid stones (5–10%) — occur in gout, leukaemia and other hyperuricaemic states, but over half of patients have no hyperuricaemia, only persistently acid urine (pH below 5.5). They are radiolucent.
  4. Cystine stones (1–2%) — caused by inherited defects in tubular reabsorption of amino acids (cystinuria), forming in acid urine.

An organic mucoprotein matrix, forming 1% to 5% of the stone by weight, is present in all calculi.

Diagnosis. Plain radiography of the abdomen (KUB) is the commonest single test because most stones (calcium and struvite) are radiopaque; ultrasonography and non-contrast CT are alternatives, CT being the most sensitive, and uric acid stones, being radiolucent, may be missed on plain films. Urinalysis shows haematuria and crystals.

Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine, either grossly visible or detected only on microscopy. Renal causes include glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, renal calculi and renal tumours such as renal cell carcinoma; post-renal causes include ureteric or bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostate carcinoma.

Complete explanation

Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of the normal, conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field in a centrifuged specimen. It is gross (macroscopic) when the urine is visibly red, smoky or cola-coloured, and microscopic when blood is detected only by dipstick or microscopy. It is one of the commonest manifestations of renal and urinary tract disease and, when painless, must always be investigated to exclude a neoplasm.

Renal causes (any four of the following)

  1. Glomerulonephritis — acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, crescentic glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome
  2. Acute pyelonephritis, and renal tuberculosis
  3. Renal calculi
  4. Renal tumours — renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour, urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
  5. Polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney
  6. Renal trauma, papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse), renal infarction, and vascular malformations

Post-renal causes (any four of the following)

  1. Ureteric calculi
  2. Bladder calculi
  3. Cystitis, including schistosomal and haemorrhagic (cyclophosphamide, radiation, adenoviral) cystitis
  4. Bladder tumours — urothelial carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma
  5. Benign prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma of the prostate; prostatitis
  6. Urethritis, urethral trauma, and instrumentation or catheterisation

Coagulation disorders and anticoagulant therapy can cause or unmask haematuria from any of these sources.

The important renal function tests are those of glomerular function — serum creatinine, blood urea, creatinine clearance and estimated GFR — and of tubular function, such as urine concentration, together with urinalysis for protein and sediment. Serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea because creatinine is produced at a constant rate from muscle, is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, and is largely unaffected by diet, hydration or liver function, whereas urea varies with all of these.

Complete explanation

Important renal function tests

  1. Glomerular filtration: serum creatinine and blood urea (BUN); creatinine clearance; estimated GFR (derived from serum creatinine, age and sex); cystatin C; inulin clearance (the reference method, used for research).
  2. Tubular function: urine specific gravity and osmolality, the concentration test after water deprivation, urinary acidification, and tests for specific tubular transport defects.
  3. Urinalysis: protein, albumin–creatinine ratio, and microscopy for red cells, casts and crystals.
  4. Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate) and acid–base status; and imaging.

Why serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea

  • Creatinine is produced from muscle creatine at a steady rate proportional to muscle mass, so its plasma level is stable; it is freely filtered at the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, with only slight tubular secretion. Its level therefore reflects GFR.
  • Urea production varies widely: it increases with high protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, catabolic states, tissue breakdown, fever and corticosteroids, and falls in liver disease and low protein intake. A large fraction of filtered urea is passively reabsorbed in the tubules, and this increases in dehydration and reduced flow, so blood urea rises in prerenal states without any parenchymal damage.
  • Creatinine is thus a more reliable index of GFR, although it is insensitive in early disease, since it rises above normal only after GFR has fallen by about half.

Bence Jones protein is free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) excreted in the urine; because the light chains are small, they are filtered by the glomerulus. It is found chiefly in multiple myeloma, and also in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, light-chain amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease and other plasma cell disorders. It is detected by urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, and classically by the heat test.

Complete explanation

What it is. Bence Jones protein consists of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, produced in excess by a neoplastic clone of plasma cells, which are small enough to be filtered at the glomerulus and appear in the urine. The reagent strip, which detects mainly albumin, may be negative, though the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive.

Conditions in which it is found

  1. Multiple myeloma (the commonest), with Bence Jones proteinuria detectable in a large proportion of patients
  2. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and other lymphoplasmacytic disorders
  3. AL amyloidosis (primary amyloidosis), in which the light chains form amyloid, and light-chain deposition disease
  4. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and occasionally chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphomas

Renal significance. In myeloma, Bence Jones proteins injure the kidney in two ways: some light chains are directly toxic to tubular epithelial cells, and others combine with Tamm–Horsfall protein under acidic conditions to form large tubular casts that obstruct the tubules and provoke a giant cell reaction (light-chain cast nephropathy, "myeloma kidney"). This is the main cause of renal dysfunction in myeloma, which develops in about half the patients; light chains also cause AL amyloidosis and light-chain deposition disease.

Laboratory detection

  1. Heat test (classic). On slow heating of acidified urine (pH about 5), the protein precipitates at 40–60 °C, redissolves partially or completely on boiling at about 100 °C, and reappears on cooling. The test is now of historical interest because it is insensitive and unreliable.
  2. Urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation. The definitive method, performed on a concentrated 24-hour urine specimen, which shows a monoclonal band and identifies its type (kappa or lambda).
  3. Serum free light-chain assay and serum protein electrophoresis, which are more sensitive.
  4. Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells.

Malignant tumours of the urinary bladder are overwhelmingly epithelial (more than 95%), the commonest being urothelial carcinoma, with squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and small cell carcinoma as less common types; mesenchymal tumours such as rhabdomyosarcoma and leiomyosarcoma are rare. The main risk factors for urothelial carcinoma are cigarette smoking, occupational exposure to aryl amines such as 2-naphthylamine, chronic infection with Schistosoma haematobium (mainly squamous carcinoma), long-term analgesic use, cyclophosphamide therapy, and pelvic irradiation.

Complete explanation

Classification of malignant bladder tumours

  1. Epithelial (over 95%)
    • Urothelial carcinoma (about 90% of bladder tumours): noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma, low grade and high grade; flat carcinoma in situ; and invasive urothelial carcinoma, with its histological variants (nested, micropapillary, plasmacytoid, sarcomatoid and others)
    • Squamous cell carcinoma (3–7% in the United States, much commoner where schistosomiasis is endemic)
    • Adenocarcinoma (rare)
    • Small cell (neuroendocrine) carcinoma (rare, very aggressive)
  2. Mesenchymal — embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) in children and leiomyosarcoma in adults
  3. Secondary — direct extension from the cervix, uterus, prostate or rectum; lymphoma; and rarely metastases

Urothelial carcinoma develops by two routes: from noninvasive papillary tumours, which arise from papillary urothelial hyperplasia, and from flat carcinoma in situ. Non–muscle-invasive papillary cancers often have activating alterations in growth factor signalling (FGFR3, RAS, PI3-kinase), recur frequently, but progress to muscle invasion in only about 20%; most muscle-invasive cancers arise from carcinoma in situ with inactivation of TP53 and RB.

Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma

  • Cigarette smoking, the most important, which increases the risk three- to seven-fold, and accounts for 50–80% of bladder cancers in men
  • Industrial exposure to aryl amines, especially 2-naphthylamine, with a latent period of 15 to 40 years
  • *Schistosoma haematobium* infection (Egypt, Sudan), which causes squamous metaplasia, dysplasia and carcinoma, mostly squamous
  • Long-term analgesic abuse (phenacetin)
  • Cyclophosphamide therapy (haemorrhagic cystitis) and pelvic irradiation
  • Male sex (male-to-female ratio 3:1), age (80% between 50 and 80 years), and urban residence; the disease is rarely familial

Diseases of the prostate

  1. Inflammation (prostatitis): acute bacterial prostatitis (usually E. coli); chronic bacterial prostatitis; chronic abacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome, the commonest form); and granulomatous prostatitis (most often after BCG instillation).

PSA, prostate-specific antigen, is a serine protease produced by the prostatic epithelium and normally secreted in semen, where it liquefies the seminal coagulum; only minute amounts circulate in normal serum. Its clinical importance is in the detection, staging and especially the follow-up of prostate cancer, although it is organ specific rather than cancer specific, and is also raised in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, infarction, and after instrumentation.

Complete explanation

PSA is an androgen-regulated serine protease secreted by prostatic epithelium whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation. In healthy men only minute amounts are found in the serum.

Clinical importance

  1. Detection and diagnosis. Elevated blood levels occur in both localised and advanced prostate cancer, and PSA is widely used with digital rectal examination to select patients for biopsy.
  2. Monitoring after treatment. Once the diagnosis has been established, serial measurement after therapy is of clear value in monitoring recurrence and disease progression.
  3. Prognosis and staging, in combination with grade and stage.

Limitations. PSA is organ specific, but not cancer specific. Serum levels are on average lower in benign prostatic hyperplasia than in cancer, but the two overlap considerably. Prostatitis, prostatic infarction, instrumentation of the prostate and ejaculation also increase PSA. Its sensitivity and specificity as a screening test are suboptimal: false-negative results occur, and many cancers are indolent, so that screening leads to overdiagnosis and overtreatment, for which reason some countries do not recommend its use for screening.

The indications for semen analysis are the evaluation of infertility in a couple, confirmation of the success of a vasectomy and the monitoring of vasectomy reversal, assessment of testicular disease or hormonal and treatment effects, screening of sperm donors and before assisted reproduction, and medicolegal purposes. The microscopic findings assessed are sperm concentration, motility, morphology and vitality, along with agglutination and the presence of white cells, red cells and immature germ cells.

Complete explanation

Indications

  1. Evaluation of male infertility, in couples unable to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse.
  2. Follow-up after vasectomy to establish azoospermia, and after vasectomy reversal or other surgery (for example varicocele repair) to assess recovery.
  3. Evaluation of testicular and hormonal disorders and follow-up of effects of chemotherapy, radiation or drugs on spermatogenesis.
  4. Selection of donors for artificial insemination and assessment before assisted reproductive procedures (IUI, IVF, ICSI), and semen cryopreservation.
  5. Medicolegal indications (rape, paternity disputes).

  • Sperm concentration and total sperm number.
  • Motility (progressive, non-progressive and immotile), assessed on a fresh preparation within an hour.
  • Vitality (live sperm by eosin–nigrosin stain), important when motility is low.
  • Morphology on a stained smear (Papanicolaou stain), assessed by strict criteria: the proportion of normal forms, and abnormalities of head, midpiece and tail.
  • Agglutination or aggregation of sperm, suggesting antisperm antibodies.
  • Round cells: leukocytes (more than 1 million per mL suggests infection, leukocytospermia) and immature germ cells; red cells, crystals and debris.

The reliability of semen analysis depends on proper collection, so the patient must be instructed as follows.

  1. Abstinence from ejaculation for a minimum of 2 days and a maximum of 7 days before collection, the period being the same for repeated samples.
  2. Collect the specimen by masturbation into a clean, sterile, wide-mouthed container provided by the laboratory, which is non-toxic to sperm. A lubricant, saliva or soap must not be used, and ordinary condoms, which contain spermicides, must not be used.

Oligospermia (oligozoospermia) is a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit, that is, below 16 million per mL (15 million per mL in the earlier WHO reference). Complete explanation

Oligospermia is a reduction in the number of spermatozoa in the ejaculate, defined as a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit (below 16 × 10⁶/mL by the WHO 2021 reference values; below 15 × 10⁶/mL in the 2010 edition). It is a common cause of male infertility, and the severity ranges from mild to severe.

Causes

  1. Varicocele, the commonest correctable cause.
  2. Cryptorchidism and other testicular atrophy (after mumps orchitis, torsion, trauma, irradiation), reflecting loss of spermatogenic tissue.
  3. Endocrine disorders: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease and androgen or anabolic steroid use.
  4. Genetic causes: Klinefelter syndrome and Y chromosome microdeletions.
  5. Drugs, toxins and heat exposure: cytotoxic drugs, alcohol, smoking, sulfasalazine, radiation, and prolonged testicular heating.

146:
Endometrial carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the female genital tract; it is diagnosed by endometrial biopsy or curettage in a woman with irregular or postmenopausal bleeding.

  • Definition: the commonest invasive cancer of the female genital tract in the US. Types: endometrioid (80-85%) and serous (~15%).
  • Diagnosis: presents with irregular or postmenopausal bleeding. There is no screening test. Diagnosis is by endometrial biopsy or curettage (histology). Ultrasound for endometrial thickness. Test endometrioid tumours for mismatch repair defects to detect Lynch syndrome.
147:
Leiomyoma is a sharply circumscribed, firm, whorled, grey-white benign smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium; its complications are abnormal bleeding, pain, infertility and pregnancy complications, and malignant change is extremely rare.

  • Gross: sharply circumscribed, round, firm, grey-white tumours with a whorled cut surface; single or multiple; intramural, submucosal or subserosal. Large ones may show yellow-brown or red softening.
  • Micro: bundles of smooth muscle with uniform oval nuclei and scant mitoses. Variants: bizarre-nuclei (FH mutation), cellular, intravenous leiomyomatosis, disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis.
  • Genetics: MED12 mutation in ~70%; HMGIC/HMGIY rearrangements; FH (HLRCC).
  • Complications: abnormal bleeding, urinary frequency, pain from infarction, infertility. In pregnancy: abortion, malpresentation, uterine inertia, postpartum haemorrhage. Malignant change is extremely rare.
149:
The hormone-producing ovarian tumours are granulosa cell tumour and thecoma (oestrogen), Sertoli-Leydig and Leydig cell tumours (androgen), struma ovarii (thyroid hormone), carcinoid (serotonin) and choriocarcinoma (hCG).

  • Oestrogen: granulosa cell tumour, thecoma. Effects: precocious puberty in children; endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma and proliferative breast disease in adults.
  • Androgen: Sertoli-Leydig and Leydig cell tumours; pregnancy luteoma may virilise.
  • Thyroid hormone: struma ovarii (hyperthyroidism).
  • Serotonin: carcinoid (carcinoid syndrome without liver metastases if large).
  • hCG: choriocarcinoma; some dysgerminomas.
  • Dermoid morphology: see Q1284.
150:
The germ cell tumours of the ovary are teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, polyembryoma and mixed tumours; a Krukenberg tumour is a bilateral ovarian metastasis of mucin-secreting signet-ring cell carcinoma, most often from the stomach.

  • Germ cell tumours (15-20% of ovarian tumours): teratoma (mature, immature, monodermal), dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, polyembryoma, mixed.
  • Krukenberg tumour: bilateral ovarian metastases of mucin-secreting signet-ring cell carcinoma, most often gastric (also colon, breast).
151:
Teratoma is a germ cell tumour showing differentiation into elements of two or more germ layers, classified as mature, immature and monodermal; Meigs syndrome is ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion.

  • Teratoma: a germ cell tumour with differentiation into elements of two or more germ layers.
  • Classification: (1) mature (benign), mostly cystic (dermoid); (2) immature (malignant), with primitive neuroepithelium; (3) monodermal/specialised (struma ovarii, carcinoid).
  • Meigs syndrome: ovarian fibroma (usually >6 cm) with ascites and pleural effusion (usually right-sided). Mechanism unknown.
152:
The gestational trophoblastic diseases are hydatidiform mole (complete and partial), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour; a mole is diagnosed by markedly raised hCG, ultrasound and histology showing swollen hydropic villi with trophoblastic hyperplasia.

  • GTD spectrum: hydatidiform mole (complete, partial), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.

  • Laboratory diagnosis:
  • hCG markedly higher than in a normal pregnancy of the same gestational age; followed for 6-12 months until non-pregnant levels.
  • Pelvic ultrasound.
  • Histology of curettage: swollen hydropic villi with trophoblastic hyperplasia.
  • Cytogenetics/ploidy and p57 IHC to separate complete from partial mole.
153:
Ectopic pregnancy refers to implantation of the gestation in a site other than the normal intrauterine location; the most common site is the fallopian tube (approximately 90% of cases). It is confirmed by an inappropriately rising hCG, pelvic sonography, endometrial biopsy and laparoscopy.

  • Definition: implantation outside the uterine cavity. Fallopian tube is the commonest site (~90%); others are ovary, abdomen, caesarean scar and cornual region.
  • Predisposing factors: chronic salpingitis from PID (35-50%), peritubal adhesions (appendicitis, endometriosis, surgery), IUCD (two-fold).
  • Clinical: abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding at 6-8 weeks. Rupture causes haemorrhagic shock, a medical emergency. It causes 4-10% of pregnancy-related deaths.
  • Confirmation: inappropriately rising hCG, pelvic sonography, endometrial biopsy (decidua without villi or trophoblast), laparoscopy.
154:
Choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblast, diagnosed by markedly raised hCG and histology showing sheets of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without villi, and it metastasises mainly to the lungs and vagina.

  • Definition: malignant neoplasm of trophoblast, arising in 1 in 20,000-30,000 pregnancies. Preceded by complete mole (50%), spontaneous abortion (25%), normal pregnancy (~22%), or ectopic pregnancy. Non-gestational choriocarcinoma (germ cell) lacks paternal DNA.
  • Morphology: soft, fleshy, yellow-white haemorrhagic and necrotic mass. Micro: sheets of malignant cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without chorionic villi, with frequent vascular invasion.
  • Diagnosis: irregular bloody spotting, markedly raised hCG, histology, and imaging for metastases.
  • Metastatic sites: lungs (50%), vagina (30-40%), then brain, liver, bone, kidney.
  • Treatment: chemotherapy gives nearly 100% remission; gestational type is curable.
762:
Fibroadenoma. It is the commonest benign breast tumour, typical at 20-30 years, presenting as a firm, rubbery, mobile, well-circumscribed lump. It is hormone-responsive.

Investigations (triple assessment)

  1. Clinical examination.
  2. Imaging: ultrasound is preferred at this age (mammography in older women); well-circumscribed density.
  3. FNAC or core biopsy: biphasic stroma and epithelium. Clinical assessment, imaging and biopsy together identify >99.5% of malignancies in symptomatic patients.
104:
Two important pituitary tumours are the prolactin-secreting lactotroph tumour (prolactinoma) and the growth hormone-secreting somatotroph tumour. Both are pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs, formerly pituitary adenomas) arising from the anterior lobe. Their significance lies in the hormone-excess syndromes they cause and in the local mass effects of an expanding sellar tumour.

Complete explanation: PitNETs are the commonest cause of hyperpituitarism. They are classified by the hormone and lineage-specific transcription factor expressed by the tumour cells (POU1F1 for somatotroph, lactotroph and thyrotroph tumours; TBX19 for corticotroph tumours; SF-1 for gonadotroph tumours). Histologically they are soft, circumscribed, composed of monotonous polygonal cells in sheets or cords with a sparse reticulin network, which distinguishes them from the mixed cell population and rich reticulin of normal anterior pituitary.

The lactotroph tumour is the most common functioning PitNET. Hyperprolactinaemia produces amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido and infertility, and is detected earlier in females than in males. Serum prolactin tends to rise in proportion to tumour size. Hyperprolactinaemia is not always due to a tumour: it also occurs in pregnancy, with dopamine-blocking drugs, with hypothyroidism and renal failure, and when any suprasellar mass interrupts the dopaminergic inhibition travelling down the pituitary stalk. Treatment is usually with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine or cabergoline).

The somatotroph tumour secretes growth hormone, which stimulates hepatic IGF-1. In children before epiphyseal closure it causes gigantism; in adults it causes acromegaly, with enlargement of the jaw, hands, feet and viscera, together with glucose intolerance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy. These tumours are often large at diagnosis because the clinical changes are insidious.

Any PitNET may cause mass effects: erosion of the sella turcica, compression of the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia), headache, hypopituitarism through destruction of normal gland, and pituitary apoplexy after haemorrhage into the tumour. A corticotroph tumour causes Cushing disease.
99:
Two benign thyroid tumours are follicular adenoma and oncocytic (Hürthle cell) adenoma. The four main malignant tumours are papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma is the most common, accounting for about 85% of thyroid cancers, and has an excellent prognosis with a 10-year survival above 95%.

Complete explanation: Follicular adenoma is a solitary, encapsulated nodule of well-differentiated follicles that compresses adjacent gland; it is diagnosed only after the capsule has been examined and found to lack invasion. A minority are functioning (toxic adenoma).

Among the malignant tumours, papillary carcinoma arises in young and middle-aged adults and spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes. Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood. Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells, about 70% sporadic and the rest in MEN-2 with germline RET mutations. Anaplastic carcinoma arises in the elderly, often from a pre-existing differentiated tumour, and is almost uniformly fatal within a year.

Prognosis of papillary carcinoma is influenced by age (worse above 55), extrathyroidal extension and distant metastasis; local recurrence occurs in 5–20% and distant spread in 10–15%.
100:
Follicular adenoma is a benign, encapsulated thyroid tumour of well-differentiated follicular cells, whereas follicular carcinoma is the malignant counterpart that shows capsular and/or vascular invasion. FNAC cannot separate them, because the cytology is identical; the distinction needs histological examination of the entire capsule.

Complete explanation: Both tumours are composed of uniform follicles containing colloid, and both commonly harbour RAS mutations. Cytologically, an aspirate from either shows cellular smears of follicular cells in microfollicles without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. The decisive feature of carcinoma is invasion: penetration of the tumour capsule, invasion of vessels within or beyond the capsule (usually veins), or invasion of adjacent thyroid.

Because this can be assessed only by extensive sampling of the capsule in the resected specimen, FNAC results are reported as "follicular neoplasm" and the nodule is surgically excised (lobectomy), with molecular testing sometimes helping to stratify indeterminate nodules. Adenomas do not recur or metastasise; follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone, lung and liver.
101:
Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormone due to overactivity of the thyroid gland. Strictly, thyrotoxicosis is the broader term and includes causes in which hormone excess does not arise from gland hyperfunction. The commonest cause is Graves disease.

Complete explanation: Types are as follows.

Associated with increased gland function (true hyperthyroidism):

  • Primary: Graves disease (diffuse hyperplasia, about 85% of cases), toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease), toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis from maternal Graves disease.
  • Secondary: TSH-secreting pituitary tumour (rare); here TSH is normal or raised.

Thyrotoxicosis without increased gland function: granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless thyroiditis, struma ovarii and factitious thyrotoxicosis from exogenous thyroxine.

In all except the pituitary type, TSH is suppressed. The clinical effects are heat intolerance, weight loss with increased appetite, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, proximal myopathy, diarrhoea and osteoporosis, with a staring gaze and lid lag from sympathetic overactivity. Radioiodine uptake distinguishes diffuse increased uptake (Graves), a hot nodule (toxic adenoma) and low uptake (thyroiditis).
102:
A young woman with a diffusely enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos has Graves disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Her thyroid hormone status will show raised free T₄ and T₃ with suppressed TSH. Hypothyroidism is the opposite state of thyroid hormone deficiency, caused most often by Hashimoto thyroiditis, iodine deficiency and iatrogenic ablation.

Complete explanation: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that stimulate the TSH receptor. Free T₄ and T₃ are elevated and TSH is suppressed; radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased and TSI/TRAb are present. The gland shows diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the epithelium with lymphoid infiltrates.

Hypothyroidism is a state of structural or functional derangement that interferes with thyroid hormone production. It is classified as primary (intrinsic thyroid disease), secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic). Common causes are Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common in iodine-sufficient regions), endemic iodine deficiency, surgical or radioiodine ablation, drugs (lithium, amiodarone, thionamides), congenital biosynthetic defects and thyroid dysgenesis.

Serum TSH is raised in primary disease and is the most sensitive screening test. In infancy, deficiency produces cretinism with intellectual disability; in adults it causes myxoedema with slowing of mental and physical activity, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, non-pitting oedema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and hypercholesterolaemia.
103:
Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It is classified by pattern into diffuse and multinodular, and by function into non-toxic (euthyroid or hypothyroid) and toxic (hyperthyroid).

Complete explanation

  1. Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goitre: the whole gland is enlarged without nodules. It is endemic (iodine deficiency, goitrogens) or sporadic (goitrogenic drugs, dyshormonogenesis, usually unknown cause). It evolves from a hyperplastic phase to a colloid involution phase.
  2. Multinodular goitre: irregular nodular enlargement resulting from recurrent hyperplasia and involution; usually euthyroid, but occasionally toxic (Plummer disease).
  3. Diffuse toxic goitre: Graves disease.
  4. Goitrous thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis with goitre.
  5. Neoplastic enlargement from a tumour.

The common mechanism is raised TSH from reduced hormone output, producing hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the follicular epithelium; in most patients the enlarged functional mass restores euthyroidism, and only when the defect is severe does goitrous hypothyroidism result. Clinical features arise mainly from mass effect.
105:
Hypoglycaemia is a fall in blood glucose to a level low enough to cause symptoms of neuroglycopenia and adrenergic activation, generally below about 3.0 mmol/L (50–54 mg/dL). In the acute situation hypoglycaemia is the more immediately dangerous, because the brain depends on a continuous glucose supply and prolonged hypoglycaemia causes irreversible neuronal injury and death within hours. Hyperglycaemia is dangerous mainly through chronic complications, although severe acute hyperglycaemia (ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state) is also life-threatening.

Complete explanation: The brain accounts for about 20% of the body's oxygen consumption and is strictly dependent on aerobic glucose metabolism, so the cellular effects of glucose deprivation resemble those of hypoxia. The cortical pyramidal neurons, the CA1 (Sommer) sector of the hippocampus and the cerebellar Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable. Clinically, hypoglycaemia presents with dizziness, confusion, sweating, palpitations and tachycardia, progressing to loss of consciousness and coma.

It most often complicates insulin or sulfonylurea therapy (missed meals, excess exercise, over-dosage), and also occurs with insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency and severe liver disease. Patients with long-standing frequent episodes may lose warning symptoms ("hypoglycaemia unawareness"), so that neurological impairment is the first sign. Rapid correction with oral or intravenous glucose prevents permanent damage.

Chronic hyperglycaemia, by contrast, damages vessels and nerves slowly over 15 to 20 years, causing nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and accelerated atherosclerosis.
106:
Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is haemoglobin A to which glucose has become non-enzymatically attached. Its level reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding two to three months, so it is the standard measure of long-term glycaemic control and is also used to diagnose diabetes.

Complete explanation: Glucose combines non-enzymatically and irreversibly with the amino terminal valine of the β-chain of HbA, and the amount formed is proportional to the prevailing glucose concentration over the life span of the red cell (about 120 days), weighted towards the most recent weeks. It is not affected by day-to-day fluctuations or by fasting. A value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic of diabetes, 5.7–6.4% indicates prediabetes, and in most diabetic patients the treatment target is below 7%.

Higher values correlate with a greater risk of microvascular complications. Results are unreliable in conditions altering red cell survival or haemoglobin structure (haemolytic anaemia, recent haemorrhage or transfusion, haemoglobinopathies, iron deficiency, chronic renal failure).
107:
A diabetic who becomes unconscious after a chest infection, omits insulin or antidiabetic treatment and has a fruity or musty odour on the breath has diabetic ketoacidosis. Urine analysis will show marked glycosuria and ketonuria.

Complete explanation: Infection raises counter-regulatory hormones (epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol) that block insulin action while insulin is absent or insufficient. The combination of insulin deficiency and glucagon excess increases gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted to ketone bodies (acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid, with acetone, which causes the odour).

Hyperglycaemia (usually 250–600 mg/dL) causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration; ketone accumulation causes metabolic acidosis with deep, laboured (Kussmaul) breathing, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and eventually coma. In the urine one finds heavy glycosuria, positive ketones on nitroprusside testing, an acid reaction and a high specific gravity; protein and pus cells may be present if there is renal involvement or infection.

Blood shows high glucose, ketonaemia, low bicarbonate and pH, raised anion gap, and a total body potassium deficit even though serum potassium may be initially raised.
108:
The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) measures the body's ability to dispose of a standard oral glucose load. After a 75 g glucose load in an adult, a two-hour plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more establishes diabetes, whereas 7.8–11.0 mmol/L defines impaired glucose tolerance. Renal glycosuria is glucose in urine despite normal blood glucose because of a low renal threshold, and alimentary glycosuria is transient glycosuria after a meal due to rapid absorption.

Complete explanation

Procedure. The patient eats an unrestricted, carbohydrate-adequate diet (at least 150 g daily) for three days and remains physically active, and fasts for 8–14 hours overnight with no smoking or exercise. A fasting blood sample is taken. The patient drinks 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in about 250–300 mL water within five minutes (1.75 g/kg up to 75 g in children). A further sample is taken at two hours, with additional samples at 30-minute intervals when a curve is wanted. Urine may be tested at each interval.

Indications. Borderline fasting glucose (impaired fasting glucose); suspected diabetes with a normal fasting value; screening for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks; unexplained glycosuria; unexplained neuropathy, retinopathy or nephropathy; and assessment of high-risk individuals such as the obese and those with a family history.

Interpretation.

Renal glycosuria: the renal tubular threshold (about 10 mmol/L or 180 mg/dL) is abnormally low (familial, pregnancy, tubular disease), so glucose appears in urine although the OGTT curve is normal.

Alimentary (lag-storage) glycosuria: rapid absorption after gastrectomy, gastroenterostomy or thyrotoxicosis produces a high early peak above the renal threshold with glycosuria, but fasting and 2-hour values are normal.
109:
Diabetes mellitus is classified by pathogenesis into type 1, type 2, other specific types and gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy.

Complete explanation

  1. Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β-cell destruction leading to absolute insulin deficiency (5–10% of cases).
  2. Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance with inadequate β-cell compensation (90–95%).
  3. Other specific types:
    • Monogenic β-cell defects: maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY, HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK and others), neonatal diabetes (KCNJ11, ABCC8), maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (mitochondrial DNA), insulin gene mutations.
    • Genetic defects of insulin action (insulin receptor mutations, type A insulin resistance).
    • Exocrine pancreatic disease ("type 3c"): chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy or trauma, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis.
    • Endocrinopathies: Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, glucagonoma, hyperthyroidism.
    • Drug- or chemical-induced: glucocorticoids, thiazides, nicotinic acid, phenytoin, β-adrenergic agonists.
    • Infections (congenital rubella, cytomegalovirus) and genetic syndromes (Down, Turner, Klinefelter).
  4. Gestational diabetes mellitus: glucose intolerance first detected in pregnancy, which occurs because pregnancy is a diabetogenic state; it usually resolves after delivery but most affected women develop overt diabetes within 10 to 20 years.
110:
The ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone. Ketonuria occurs whenever fat is being oxidised faster than the tissues can use the ketones formed, most importantly in uncontrolled diabetes, but also in starvation and prolonged vomiting.

Complete explanation: Ketone bodies are produced in hepatic mitochondria from acetyl coenzyme A derived from fatty acids; β-hydroxybutyrate is quantitatively the main one in ketoacidosis, whereas the routine nitroprusside (Rothera) test detects acetoacetate and acetone only. They are normally used as fuel by muscle, heart and brain, and when production outstrips use they appear in blood (ketonaemia) and urine (ketonuria).

Causes of ketonuria:

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (insulin deficiency).
  • Starvation, prolonged fasting, very low carbohydrate diet.
  • Persistent vomiting (hyperemesis of pregnancy, pyloric stenosis) and severe diarrhoea.
  • Alcoholic ketoacidosis; febrile illness in children; thyrotoxicosis.
  • Glycogen storage diseases, and treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
111:
Diabetic ketoacidosis develops when a profound deficiency of insulin, together with excess glucagon and other stress hormones, causes unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone production, together with severe hyperglycaemia and osmotic dehydration. It is mainly a complication of type 1 diabetes.

Complete explanation: The usual precipitant is omission of insulin, or infection, trauma or other stress. Epinephrine and other stress hormones antagonise residual insulin and stimulate glucagon secretion. The glucagon-to-insulin imbalance reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, so that plasma glucose rises to 250–600 mg/dL. Glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis, loss of water and electrolytes and dehydration.

Insulin deficiency also activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, which releases free fatty acids. In the liver these are converted to fatty acyl coenzyme A and oxidised to acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid. The rate of formation exceeds peripheral use, causing ketonaemia and ketonuria. When dehydration limits renal excretion of ketones, systemic metabolic acidosis results. Protein catabolism supplies ketogenic amino acids and aggravates the process.

Patients present with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath and Kussmaul respiration, and become drowsy and comatose if untreated. Ketoacidosis is less frequent in type 2 diabetes because the higher portal insulin level restrains hepatic fatty acid oxidation; type 2 patients are more liable to a hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Treatment consists of insulin, fluid and electrolyte replacement and correction of the precipitating cause.
112:
Type 2 diabetes results from the combination of insulin resistance in peripheral tissues and a failure of the pancreatic β cells to compensate, producing relative insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility and obesity, especially visceral obesity, are the main determinants.

Complete explanation: There is no autoimmune basis.

Genetic factors. Concordance in monozygotic twins exceeds 90%, and first-degree relatives have a 5- to 10-fold increased risk. Genome-wide studies have identified more than 30 loci (such as TCF7L2) of modest effect, many involved in β-cell function, adipose tissue function and obesity.

Insulin resistance. Insulin resistance usually precedes hyperglycaemia. Its consequences are failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (high fasting glucose), reduced glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis in skeletal muscle after meals (high postprandial glucose), and uncontrolled lipolysis in adipose tissue (high free fatty acids). Defects include reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of the insulin receptor and IRS proteins and decreased GLUT-4 translocation.

Obesity contributes through several mechanisms: excess free fatty acids that generate toxic lipid intermediates (diacylglycerol, ceramides) and impair insulin signalling; altered adipokines with lowered adiponectin; chronic inflammation, in which fatty acids activate the inflammasome and release IL-1β and other cytokines; and hepatic steatosis (MASLD).

β-cell dysfunction. Initially the β cells hypersecrete and hyperinsulinaemia maintains euglycaemia. Eventually they fail, through lipotoxicity from excess fatty acids, glucotoxicity, a blunted incretin effect (reduced GIP and GLP-1 action), and islet amyloid deposition (found in over 90% of long-standing cases), together with genetic effects on insulin secretion.

Other risk factors are a sedentary lifestyle, sleep disorders and circadian disruption. The combination of obesity, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension is the metabolic syndrome.
113:
The macroscopic (macrovascular) complications of diabetes result from accelerated atherosclerosis of the aorta and large and medium-sized arteries, causing myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral vascular disease with gangrene. Hypoglycaemic coma is unconsciousness from a fall in blood glucose, usually due to excessive insulin or sulfonylurea dosage.

Complete explanation: Persistent hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance cause widespread endothelial dysfunction, which predisposes to atherosclerosis that is histologically identical to that in non-diabetics but occurs earlier and more severely. Hypertension and dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides and LDL, low HDL) potentiate it. Myocardial infarction is the most common cause of death in diabetes and is almost as common in diabetic women as in men. Cerebrovascular disease and renal artery atherosclerosis follow, and gangrene of the lower limbs is about 100 times more frequent than in the general population.

Gross renal changes include diffuse granular, contracted kidneys from arteriolosclerosis and nephrosclerosis, and pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis.

The microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) are due to diffuse basement-membrane thickening and increased capillary permeability.

Hypoglycaemic coma follows missed meals, exertion or inappropriate dosing; the patient is cold, pale and sweating with tachycardia and hunger, then confused and unconscious. It requires immediate oral or intravenous glucose, since prolonged hypoglycaemia causes permanent neuronal damage, especially of the cortex and hippocampus.
114:
Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the feature of hyperglycaemia caused by defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or most commonly both. By WHO and ADA criteria it is diagnosed by a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, a two-hour OGTT value or random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more with classic symptoms, or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more.

Complete explanation: The chronic hyperglycaemia causes secondary damage in the kidneys, eyes, nerves and blood vessels, and diabetes is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease, blindness and non-traumatic amputation. Diagnostic criteria (any one; all except a symptomatic random glucose must be confirmed on a separate day, and if two tests disagree the more abnormal result is accepted):

  1. Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).
  2. Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms.
  3. Two-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75 g OGTT.
  4. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.

Acute stresses such as infection, burns or trauma can cause transient hyperglycaemia, so persistence after recovery is required.
115:
These are the descriptive terms used for primary skin lesions. Macules and patches are flat lesions distinguished only by colour, the macule being less than 5 mm and the patch larger. Papules are solid elevations less than 5 mm. Vesicles and bullae are fluid-filled blisters, smaller and larger than 5 mm respectively. A pustule is a pus-filled elevation, and a wheal is a transient, oedematous, pale-pink raised plaque.

Complete explanation: Dermatopathology begins with a precise clinical vocabulary, because the distribution and character of a lesion often point to the diagnosis before any tissue is examined.

TermDefinition
MaculeFlat, circumscribed area of colour change, less than 5 mm in diameter.
PatchA flat lesion of altered colour larger than 5 mm.
PapuleSolid, elevated, dome-shaped or flat-topped lesion less than 5 mm in diameter.
VesicleFluid-filled, raised lesion less than 5 mm in diameter, lying within or just beneath the epidermis.
BullaA fluid-filled, raised lesion larger than 5 mm.

PustuleDiscrete, raised lesion filled with pus, i.e. neutrophils and debris.

A plaque is the larger counterpart of the papule: an elevated, flat-topped lesion greater than 5 mm in diameter, usually produced by confluent papules. The size limit of 5 mm is the conventional dividing line between each small and large pair.
116:
The skin consists of the epidermis, the dermis and the subcutis, with appendages such as hair follicles and sweat and sebaceous glands. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium of basal, spinous, granular and cornified layers. Parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, hypergranulosis is thickening of the granular layer, acanthosis is thickening of the epidermis from hyperplasia of the spinous layer, and spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis.

Complete explanation

Structure of the skin. The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium whose principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves upward from the basal layer. The deepest layer, the stratum basale, is a single row of cuboidal cells attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes; it contains the proliferating stem cells. Above it lies the stratum spinosum, whose cells are joined by desmosomes, giving the spiny appearance on fixation.

Next is the stratum granulosum, with coarse basophilic keratohyalin granules that contribute to the cornified envelope. The outermost layer, the stratum corneum, consists of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames that form the barrier; on the palms and soles a clear stratum lucidum may be identified. Interspersed among the keratinocytes are melanocytes in the basal layer, which transfer melanin to neighbouring keratinocytes and protect the nuclei from ultraviolet radiation, Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting dendritic cells in the spinous layer, and Merkel cells, which are touch-related neuroendocrine cells.

The epidermis is separated from the dermis by the basement membrane zone, which anchors it and whose components (hemidesmosomal proteins, laminin, type VII collagen) are targeted in several blistering diseases. The dermis has a superficial papillary layer of loose connective tissue containing capillary loops, and a deeper, denser reticular layer of thick collagen bundles and elastic fibres, with blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves and sensory receptors.

The subcutis is composed of lobules of fat separated by fibrous septa. The appendages (pilosebaceous units, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands, and nails) arise from the epidermis and extend into the dermis.

Descriptive terms

  • Parakeratosis is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. It indicates rapid epidermal turnover with incomplete maturation of keratinocytes, and it is accompanied by a thin or absent granular layer, as in psoriasis.
  • Hypergranulosis is an increase in the thickness of the stratum granulosum, usually a response to chronic rubbing or scratching, and a prominent feature of lichen planus.
  • Acanthosis is diffuse epithelial hyperplasia, with thickening of the stratum spinosum, and is a common response to chronic irritation or growth factors.
  • Spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis. The oedema stretches the intercellular bridges so that the keratinocytes are pulled apart; it is the hallmark of eczematous dermatitis, and when severe it forms intraepidermal vesicles.

Related terms that complete the group are hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum), acantholysis (loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes, as in pemphigus), and dyskeratosis (premature, abnormal keratinisation of individual cells).
117:
The blistering diseases of the skin are classified by the level at which the blister forms. Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus form intraepidermal blisters through acantholysis. Bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa and porphyria cutanea tarda form subepidermal blisters. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and impetigo produce subcorneal blisters.

Complete explanation: In vesiculobullous disease, a blister arises either within the epidermis, from damage to desmosomes and keratinocyte cohesion, or beneath it, from damage to the basement membrane zone. The distinction is clinically important because intraepidermal blisters have a thin roof and rupture easily, producing erosions, whereas subepidermal blisters have a full-thickness roof and remain tense and intact.

118:
The important premalignant conditions of the skin are actinic (solar) keratosis, Bowen disease, arsenical and radiation keratoses, xeroderma pigmentosum, leukoplakia of mucosal surfaces, long-standing scars and chronic ulcers, and the dysplastic naevus.

Complete explanation: Many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas, and a proportion of melanomas, arise from recognisable precursor lesions in which cumulative DNA damage has already produced cytological atypia.

  • Actinic keratosis is the commonest premalignant lesion. It appears on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned older people as a small, rough, scaly erythematous or brown patch. Microscopically there is atypia of the basal keratinocytes with parakeratosis and solar elastosis in the dermis. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is uncommon for any single lesion but cumulatively significant.
  • Bowen disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ, with full-thickness epidermal atypia but an intact basement membrane.
  • Arsenical keratosis and radiation dermatitis result from chemical or ionising carcinogen exposure and are followed by squamous carcinoma after a long latent interval.
  • Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive defect of nucleotide excision repair, producing multiple cancers at a young age on exposure to sunlight.
  • Leukoplakia and lichen sclerosus of the oral or genital mucosa carry a risk of squamous carcinoma.
  • Chronic scars, burn scars, sinus tracts and non-healing ulcers may give rise to squamous carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).
  • Dysplastic naevus, particularly in the familial dysplastic naevus syndrome, is both a marker of increased risk and a precursor of melanoma.
119:
The important tumours of the skin include benign tumours such as seborrhoeic keratosis, naevi, adnexal tumours and dermatofibroma, and malignant tumours such as squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and malignant melanoma, together with Kaposi sarcoma and cutaneous lymphoma. The locally malignant tumour of the skin is basal cell carcinoma.
