Their grade, depth, size and resectability determine prognosis.
136:
Meningitis is inflammation of the leptomeninges, the pia and arachnoid, with an inflammatory exudate in the cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space. It may be acute pyogenic (bacterial), aseptic (usually viral) or chronic (tuberculous or fungal). The causative organisms depend on the age of the patient: Escherichia coli and group B streptococci in neonates, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae in infants and children, and N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae in adolescents, adults and the elderly.

Complete explanation: Meningitis is defined as inflammation of the leptomeninges and of the subarachnoid CSF. Microorganisms reach the meninges mostly by the haematogenous route, from an infected focus such as the nasopharynx or lung, and less often by direct spread from otitis media, mastoiditis or sinusitis, by direct implantation through a skull fracture or neurosurgery, or by a congenital neural tube defect. Because the CSF has little immune defence, bacteria that enter it multiply freely, and the inflammatory response, rather than the organism alone, produces much of the damage.

Causes

TypeOrganisms
Acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitisNeonates: Escherichia coli, group B streptococci (Streptococcus agalactiae), Listeria monocytogenes. Infants and children: Haemophilus influenzae type b (now much less frequent after vaccination), Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae. Adolescents and young adults: N. meningitidis. Elderly: S. pneumoniae, Listeria, gram-negative bacilli.
Acute lymphocytic (aseptic) meningitisViruses: enteroviruses (coxsackie, echovirus), mumps, herpes simplex virus 2, HIV, arboviruses.
Chronic meningitisMycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans and other fungi, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia burgdorferi.

Grossly in acute pyogenic meningitis, a creamy-yellow exudate lies within the subarachnoid space over the brain surface, especially around the sulci and the base. Microscopically there are neutrophils in the subarachnoid space, and in severe cases the exudate extends along the perivascular spaces and causes ventriculitis, vasculitis, thrombophlebitis and cerebral oedema. Complications include hydrocephalus, cerebral infarction, and cranial nerve palsies. Clinically there is fever, headache, photophobia, irritability, neck stiffness and altered consciousness.
133:
Tumours of the central nervous system are classified by their cell of origin into gliomas (astrocytic, oligodendroglial and ependymal), neuronal and glioneuronal tumours, choroid plexus tumours, embryonal tumours such as medulloblastoma, tumours of the meninges, nerve sheath tumours, germ cell tumours, primary CNS lymphoma, sellar tumours, and metastases. Their peculiarities are that the site matters more than the histological grade, that benign tumours can be lethal because of the closed cranium, that infiltrating gliomas cannot be cured by excision, and that they rarely metastasise outside the CNS but may spread through the CSF.

Complete explanation

Classification. The classification of the World Health Organisation (2021) combines histology with molecular markers and grades the tumours from 1 to 4.

GroupExamples
Adult-type diffuse gliomasAstrocytoma, IDH-mutant (grades 2–4); oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted (grades 2–3); glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (grade 4)
Circumscribed astrocytic gliomas and paediatric-type gliomasPilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1), paediatric-type diffuse gliomas
Ependymal tumoursEpendymoma
Glioneuronal and neuronal tumoursGanglioglioma, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour, central neurocytoma
Choroid plexus tumoursChoroid plexus papilloma and carcinoma
Embryonal tumoursMedulloblastoma, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour
Tumours of cranial and paraspinal nervesSchwannoma, neurofibroma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
MeningiomasMeningioma (grades 1–3)
Haematolymphoid tumoursPrimary CNS lymphoma
Germ cell tumoursGerminoma and others
Sellar region tumoursPituitary neuroendocrine tumours, craniopharyngioma
Metastatic tumoursCarcinomas of lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, and colon

Metastases are the commonest brain tumours in adults. Among primary tumours, glioblastoma is the most frequent in adults and pilocytic astrocytoma and medulloblastoma are common in children.

Peculiarities of CNS tumours.

  1. The location is as important as the histology. Because the skull and spinal canal are rigid, even a histologically benign tumour compresses vital structures, raises intracranial pressure, and may cause herniation or hydrocephalus and death.
  2. Distinction between benign and malignant is not absolute. Grading depends on biological behaviour and now on molecular features; a low-grade tumour in the brainstem can be fatal, whereas some malignant types are slow.
  3. Diffusely infiltrating gliomas invade the brain beyond the visible margin and cannot be completely excised, so they recur even after surgery.
  4. Extracranial metastasis is rare, because the CNS has no lymphatics and the tumour rarely invades the venous sinuses, but tumours such as medulloblastoma and ependymoma spread through the CSF as "drop metastases".
  5. Age and site distribution: infratentorial tumours predominate in children, and supratentorial tumours in adults.
  6. Progression: low-grade gliomas may progress to higher grades.
  7. The blood–brain barrier limits the access of chemotherapy.
  8. Presentation is with seizures, focal deficits, or features of raised intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, papilloedema).
134:
A meningioma is a usually benign, slow-growing tumour arising from the arachnoid cap cells of the meninges. It is attached to the dura and compresses the brain without invading it. The peripheral nerve sheath tumours are schwannoma, neurofibroma, and the malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour.

Complete explanation

Meningioma. It is a tumour of the arachnoid (meningothelial) cells, commonly seen in adults, with a peak in the sixth and seventh decades, and more often in women. Inactivation of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 (loss of merlin) is the commonest genetic abnormality, and the risk is raised by ionising radiation and in neurofibromatosis type 2. They occur along the dural surfaces, most often over the cerebral convexities, parasagittal region, falx, sphenoid wing and olfactory groove, and in the spinal canal.

Gross. A round or lobulated, firm, well-circumscribed, dural-based mass that indents the brain but is separated from it, and has a grey-white cut surface. It may invade the overlying bone, causing hyperostosis. "En plaque" tumours spread as a flat sheet along the dura.

Microscopic. Meningothelial (syncytial) tumours show lobules of cells with oval nuclei, and concentric whorls of cells. The fibroblastic type has spindle cells in parallel bundles, and the transitional type shows features of both. In the psammomatous type, the whorls undergo calcification, forming psammoma bodies. Most meningiomas are WHO grade 1; atypical (grade 2) meningiomas show increased mitoses, and anaplastic (grade 3) tumours are overtly malignant with brain invasion. Meningiomas are positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors.

Clinical. Slow growth gives headache, seizures and focal signs due to compression. On imaging, they enhance strongly and show a "dural tail". Complete excision is curative, but atypical tumours recur.

Peripheral nerve sheath tumours.

  1. Schwannoma: a benign, encapsulated tumour of Schwann cells; it commonly affects the vestibular nerve at the cerebellopontine angle (acoustic neuroma), and bilateral tumours characterise NF2. Microscopically, it shows compact Antoni A areas with palisading nuclei (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas; the cells are S100-positive.
  2. Neurofibroma: a benign tumour made of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, perineurial cells and mast cells in a myxoid or collagenous matrix, which may be cutaneous or plexiform; plexiform neurofibromas are characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1 mutation) and can undergo malignant change.
  3. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour: a sarcoma arising from a nerve or a plexiform neurofibroma, especially in NF1, with spindle cells, mitoses and necrosis.
135:
The glial tumours of the CNS are the astrocytic tumours, which include the diffuse astrocytoma, glioblastoma and pilocytic astrocytoma; the oligodendroglioma; and the ependymoma.

Complete explanation

  1. Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant (grades 2–4). A diffusely infiltrating tumour of adults, with mutation of IDH1 or IDH2, which transforms to higher grades.
  2. Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (grade 4). The most common and most malignant primary brain tumour of adults, with a poor prognosis. It forms a necrotic, haemorrhagic mass in the cerebral hemisphere, with pleomorphic astrocytes, necrosis with pseudopalisading of tumour cells and microvascular proliferation; common molecular features include EGFR amplification, TERT promoter mutation, and gain of chromosome 7 with loss of chromosome 10. It crosses the corpus callosum ("butterfly glioma").
  3. Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1). A circumscribed, slow-growing tumour in children and young adults, typically in the cerebellum, often cystic with a mural nodule. It shows bipolar cells with Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies, and is associated with BRAF alterations. It is usually cured by excision.
  4. Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted (grades 2–3). Occurs in the cerebral hemispheres of adults, with round uniform nuclei and perinuclear halos ("fried-egg" cells), a delicate network of capillaries ("chicken-wire"), and calcification. It is more responsive to chemotherapy.
  5. Ependymoma. Arises from the ependymal lining of the ventricles or the central canal of the spinal cord; in children it occurs in the fourth ventricle, and in adults in the spinal cord. It shows perivascular pseudorosettes and true ependymal rosettes, and may obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.
137:
A cataract is an opacification of the lens of the eye that interferes with the transmission of light, and is the commonest cause of reversible blindness. The commonest cause is ageing (senile cataract). Other causes include congenital infections such as rubella, metabolic disorders such as diabetes mellitus and galactosaemia, drugs especially corticosteroids, trauma, ultraviolet and ionising radiation, uveitis and smoking.

Complete explanation: The normal lens is transparent because its fibres are arranged in an orderly fashion and contain soluble crystallin proteins. A cataract develops when these proteins aggregate and denature, producing light-scattering opacities. Oxidative damage, accumulated with age, cross-links and aggregates the crystallins, and the lens fibres degenerate, so the lens becomes cloudy, and later yellow or brown.

Causes

  1. Ageing (senile cataract): by far the most common type. Nuclear, cortical and posterior subcapsular opacities occur.
  2. Congenital cataract: intrauterine infections (rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis), chromosomal syndromes such as Down syndrome, and galactosaemia.
  3. Metabolic disease: diabetes mellitus, in which excess glucose is converted by aldose reductase to sorbitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes osmotic swelling and damage; galactosaemia, through galactitol accumulation; and hypocalcaemia.
  4. Drugs: long-term corticosteroids, and others such as chlorpromazine.
  5. Physical agents: trauma, ultraviolet and ionising radiation, and heat (glassblowers).
  6. Ocular disease: chronic uveitis, glaucoma and high myopia.
  7. Smoking and excess alcohol, as risk factors.

Morphology. Microscopically there is swelling and liquefaction of lens fibres, forming eosinophilic globules (Morgagnian globules) and clefts, with epithelial proliferation and abnormal migration beneath the capsule. The clinical effect is a progressive painless loss of vision, and treatment is surgical removal of the lens, with insertion of an intraocular lens.
138:
Retinoblastoma is the commonest primary intraocular malignant tumour of childhood. It arises from primitive retinal cells and is caused by loss of both copies of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14. Microscopically it is composed of undifferentiated small round blue cells with Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes and areas of necrosis and calcification. The usual presentation is leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex.

Complete explanation: Retinoblastoma is the commonest primary intraocular malignancy in children, presenting usually before the age of 5 years. About 60% of cases are sporadic and unilateral; about 40% are hereditary, and these are frequently bilateral or multifocal. It is the prototype of Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. In the hereditary form, one mutant RB1 allele is inherited in every cell (the first hit), and the second allele is lost somatically in retinal cells (the second hit), with an almost complete penetrance, whereas in the sporadic form both mutations occur somatically in one retinal cell.

The loss of RB protein releases E2F transcription factors, causing unregulated cell cycle progression. Patients with the hereditary form are also at risk of second primary tumours, especially osteosarcoma and soft tissue sarcomas, and of pineoblastoma (trilateral retinoblastoma).

Morphology. Grossly, the tumour is a soft, chalky white to grey mass arising in the retina. It may grow inward into the vitreous (endophytic), outward under the retina to cause detachment (exophytic), or both, and fragments seed into the vitreous and anterior chamber. Areas of necrosis and chalky calcification are frequent.

Microscopically, the tumour consists of sheets of undifferentiated small round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, scanty cytoplasm and brisk mitotic activity. Characteristic rosettes are present: Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes, a ring of cuboidal or columnar cells around a central lumen, which are specific to the tumour and reflect photoreceptor differentiation; Homer Wright rosettes, in which cells surround a central tangle of fibrils; and fleurettes, which indicate photoreceptor differentiation and a better differentiated tumour.

Large areas of necrosis occur where the tumour outgrows its blood supply, and calcified DNA from necrotic cells is deposited around the vessels, which are often surrounded by a cuff of viable tumour cells.

Spread and clinical features. The tumour extends along the optic nerve into the brain and subarachnoid space, invades the choroid and sclera, and spreads by the blood stream to bone and other organs. The usual presenting sign is leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex), with strabismus, a red painful eye or poor vision. With early detection and treatment (enucleation, chemotherapy, laser and cryotherapy, radiotherapy), over 90% of patients are cured.
155:
A biopsy is the removal of a sample of living tissue from the body for histopathological examination, to establish or confirm a diagnosis.

Types of biopsy

  • Incisional biopsy: only a representative part of the lesion is removed.
  • Excisional biopsy: the entire lesion is removed with a margin of normal tissue.
  • Punch biopsy (skin, cervix), needle (core/Tru-cut) biopsy (liver, kidney, breast, prostate) and fine-needle aspiration (FNAC, cytology).
  • Endoscopic biopsy (stomach, colon, bronchus, bladder), curettage (endometrium) and shave biopsy (skin).
  • Frozen section (intra-operative) biopsy for rapid diagnosis during surgery.

Steps of preparation for routine histopathology

  1. Receiving and gross examination of the specimen, with labelling and description.
  2. Fixation in 10% neutral buffered formalin.
  3. Grossing and tissue processing: dehydration in graded alcohol, clearing in xylene, and infiltration with molten paraffin wax.
  4. Embedding in paraffin blocks.
  5. Section cutting (3–5 µm) with a microtome and floating the sections on slides.
  6. Staining with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) after removing wax and rehydrating.
  7. Mounting with a coverslip, followed by microscopic examination and reporting.
156:
Fixatives are used to preserve tissue in as lifelike a state as possible by preventing autolysis and putrefaction, and to harden it so that it can be processed and cut into thin sections.

Importance of fixatives

  1. They prevent autolysis (self-digestion by tissue enzymes) and bacterial decomposition.
  2. They stabilise cellular proteins and preserve cell and tissue structure with minimal distortion.
  3. They harden the tissue, which makes thin section cutting possible.
  4. They improve the staining and optical differentiation of cell components.
  5. They kill pathogenic organisms and make the specimen safe to handle.

The commonest fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin (volume of fixative 10–20 times the volume of tissue, fixation for 6–24 hours). Others are Bouin fluid, Carnoy fluid, glutaraldehyde (electron microscopy) and alcohol (cytology). Delayed or inadequate fixation causes poor staining and artefacts.
157:
A biopsy specimen is sent immediately in a container with adequate 10% neutral buffered formalin (10–20 times the tissue volume), together with a properly completed request form; stains used routinely are haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), with special stains when needed.

How to send the specimen

  1. Place the tissue promptly in a wide-mouthed, leak-proof container with 10% formalin, so that it is completely submerged. For frozen section, send fresh, unfixed tissue immediately.
  2. Label the container with the patient's name, age, sex, registration number, site and date.
  3. Fill in the request form: clinical history, examination findings, investigation results, site and nature of the specimen, provisional diagnosis, and the surgeon's name.
  4. Send the whole specimen; large organs are incised to allow fixative to penetrate, and surgical margins are marked with sutures or ink.
  5. Transport without delay and in a secure way.

Stains used in histopathology

  • H&E: routine stain; nuclei blue-purple, cytoplasm and collagen pink.
  • Special stains: PAS (glycogen, fungi, mucin), Masson trichrome and van Gieson (collagen), reticulin (silver), Perls Prussian blue (iron), Congo red (amyloid), Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast bacilli), Gram stain, Gomori methenamine silver (fungi), Alcian blue (mucin), Sudan/Oil red O (fat, frozen sections).
  • Immunohistochemistry for tumour typing and prognostic markers.
158:
Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis (reactive hyperplasia) shows enlarged lymph nodes with preserved architecture and a mixed, reactive proliferation of lymphoid cells, in one of three patterns: follicular hyperplasia, paracortical hyperplasia or sinus histiocytosis.

Morphology

  • Gross: the nodes are enlarged, firm, discrete, mobile and grey-white, and the capsule is intact.
  • Follicular hyperplasia: enlarged, numerous and irregular reactive follicles (secondary follicles) with germinal centres showing a polarised zonation of dark and light zones, tingible-body macrophages, mitoses, and a surrounding mantle zone. The follicles are separated by normal interfollicular tissue. It is seen in rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis and early HIV infection.
  • Paracortical hyperplasia: expansion of the T-cell zone with immunoblasts, seen in viral infections (infectious mononucleosis) and drug reactions.
  • Sinus histiocytosis: distended sinuses filled with benign histiocytes, seen in nodes draining cancers.
  • The key feature that separates reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma is preservation of the nodal architecture, with a polymorphous population of cells.
159:
The commonest causes of generalised lymphadenopathy in a 60-year-old are lymphoma (non-Hodgkin and Hodgkin) and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, with tuberculosis, metastatic carcinoma and HIV infection among the important alternatives.

Differential diagnosis

  • Neoplastic: non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, acute leukaemia, and metastatic carcinoma.
  • Infective: tuberculosis, HIV, infectious mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, brucellosis, syphilis, and kala-azar.
  • Autoimmune and others: systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, drug reactions (phenytoin), and amyloidosis.

Investigations

  1. Complete blood count and peripheral blood film (lymphocytosis, blasts, atypical cells), ESR.
  2. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a node, followed by an excision lymph node biopsy (the investigation of choice) with histopathology and immunohistochemistry.
  3. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy; flow cytometry.
  4. Chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, CT scan for staging and mediastinal or abdominal nodes.
  5. Mantoux test, sputum for AFB, HIV and viral serology, LDH, liver and renal function tests.
160:
Firm cervical lymphadenopathy with evening rise of temperature and weight loss most probably indicates tuberculous lymphadenitis; lymphoma (especially Hodgkin lymphoma) is the important differential diagnosis.

Investigations

  1. Complete blood count (lymphocytosis), raised ESR, Mantoux test, chest X-ray (pulmonary tuberculosis), and sputum for acid-fast bacilli.
  2. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC): epithelioid cell granulomas, caseous necrosis and Langhans giant cells; Ziehl–Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli; CBNAAT (GeneXpert) and culture.
  3. Excision biopsy of the lymph node if FNAC is inconclusive: caseating granulomas with central caseous necrosis, epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and a rim of lymphocytes.
  4. Interferon-gamma release assay and HIV testing; imaging when needed.
  5. Biopsy and immunohistochemistry to exclude lymphoma (Reed–Sternberg cells in Hodgkin lymphoma).
161:
A child with sore throat and a single tender submandibular lymph node most probably has acute nonspecific (suppurative) lymphadenitis secondary to acute tonsillitis or pharyngitis, usually streptococcal.

The node enlarges because it drains the infected tonsil and pharynx. It is swollen, tender, painful and slightly red; there may be fever. Histologically, there is congestion of the sinuses, neutrophil infiltration, and reactive follicular hyperplasia with large germinal centres; severe infection may form an abscess with necrosis and pus (suppurative lymphadenitis).

Treatment is with antibiotics for the throat infection, and the node regresses as infection resolves.
162:
Fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain in a 5-year-old girl most probably indicate acute bacterial pneumonia (lobar pneumonia or bronchopneumonia), usually due to Streptococcus pneumoniae; pleuritic pain indicates involvement of the pleura.

Morphological changes in the lungs (stages of lobar pneumonia)

  1. Congestion (day 1–2): heavy, red, boggy lung; vascular engorgement, intra-alveolar fluid with few neutrophils and many bacteria.
  2. Red hepatisation (day 2–4): firm, red, liver-like lung; alveoli filled with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin; fibrinous pleuritis.
  3. Grey hepatisation (day 4–8): grey-brown, firm lung; red cells lysed, with a fibrinopurulent exudate of neutrophils and fibrin.
  4. Resolution (day 8–10 onward): enzymatic digestion of the exudate, which is liquefied and cleared by macrophages, cough and lymphatics.

In bronchopneumonia there are patchy consolidated foci around bronchi.

Complications: lung abscess, empyema, pleural effusion, organisation of the exudate (carnification), bacteraemia with meningitis, arthritis or endocarditis, and respiratory failure.
163:
The diagnosis is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), mainly chronic bronchitis, because the patient is a smoker with a productive cough on most days for at least three months in two consecutive years, with recurrent episodes and breathlessness.

COPD is a group of chronic diffuse airway diseases with obstruction to airflow, and the diseases included are:

  1. Chronic bronchitis: persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years; hypertrophy of mucous glands (increased Reid index) and goblet cell hyperplasia.
  2. Emphysema: permanent abnormal enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of their walls (centriacinar, panacinar, paraseptal types).
  3. Chronic asthmatic bronchitis (asthma with a chronic obstructive component).
  4. Bronchiectasis and small airway disease (chronic bronchiolitis) are also grouped with obstructive diseases.

Cigarette smoking is the major cause. Diagnosis is by spirometry (FEV₁/FVC below 70%, not fully reversible).
164:
A smoker with cough, chest pain, haemoptysis and breathlessness for 3 months, with a homogeneous opacity and pleural effusion, most probably has bronchogenic carcinoma of the lung (squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma) with malignant pleural effusion.

Investigations available in a medical college

  1. Imaging: chest X-ray, CT scan of the chest.
  2. Sputum cytology for malignant cells (best for central tumours).
  3. Bronchoscopy with bronchial brushings, washings and biopsy for histopathology.
  4. Pleural fluid: aspiration for cytology, cell count, protein and LDH (usually a haemorrhagic exudate), and pleural biopsy.
  5. Image-guided FNAC or core needle biopsy of peripheral lesions; FNAC of enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  6. Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma), p40 and p63 (squamous cell carcinoma), neuroendocrine markers (small cell carcinoma).
  7. Staging: CT of the abdomen and brain, bone scan, and routine tests (CBC, ESR, liver function tests, serum calcium).
169:
The specimens taken to diagnose different lung lesions depend on the type of lesion, and they include cytological and tissue specimens.

Cytology

  • Sputum: for malignant cells and for acid-fast bacilli, fungi and bacteria.
  • Bronchial washings and brushings during bronchoscopy.
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage: for infection (Pneumocystis), and interstitial lung disease.
  • Pleural fluid: for malignant cells, cell count and biochemistry.
  • FNAC: percutaneous (CT- or ultrasound-guided) for peripheral lesions.

Tissue (histopathology)

  • Bronchoscopic (endobronchial) biopsy for central tumours.
  • Transbronchial lung biopsy for diffuse parenchymal and peripheral lesions.
  • Percutaneous core needle biopsy for peripheral masses.
  • Pleural biopsy (Abram needle or thoracoscopic) for pleural disease.
  • Open or video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy for interstitial lung diseases, and lobectomy or pneumonectomy specimens for resected tumours.
  • Lymph node biopsy (mediastinoscopy, EBUS-guided) for staging.
165:
A firm, slowly growing parotid swelling for 2 years in a 50-year-old woman is most probably a pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumour), and it is diagnosed by clinical examination, FNAC and histopathology of the excised specimen.

Proceed as follows

  1. Clinical examination: painless, firm, mobile, lobulated swelling; check facial nerve function (facial palsy suggests malignancy), fixity to skin and cervical lymph nodes.
  2. FNAC: gives a preoperative diagnosis; shows epithelial cells and fibrillary chondromyxoid stroma (magenta on Giemsa).
  3. Imaging: ultrasound, CT or MRI to show extent and relation to the facial nerve.
  4. Excision (superficial parotidectomy) with the specimen sent for histopathology; enucleation is avoided because of recurrence.

Histology of pleomorphic adenoma: a capsulated tumour of epithelial cells (ductal and myoepithelial) in sheets and ducts, with a chondromyxoid stroma and sometimes areas of cartilage. Other possibilities are Warthin tumour, mucoepidermoid carcinoma and adenoid cystic carcinoma.
166:
Epigastric pain after meals in a 50-year-old woman, with an abnormality seen on upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (the question text is incomplete in the bank), suggests a gastric ulcer, and the main differential diagnosis is gastric carcinoma; a gastric biopsy is needed to distinguish them.

Gastric (peptic) ulcer: a solitary, round to oval, punched-out ulcer (usually on the lesser curvature near the angular notch) with a clean base and straight, sharply cut margins; the surrounding mucosal folds radiate to the ulcer edge. Microscopically, the base shows four layers: necrotic fibrinopurulent debris, nonspecific inflammatory infiltrate, granulation tissue, and fibrous scar. The most common cause is Helicobacter pylori infection, along with NSAIDs.

Gastric carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, intestinal or diffuse type) may present as an ulcer with heaped-up, irregular margins and a necrotic base. It must be excluded by taking multiple biopsies from the ulcer margin and base.

Investigations: endoscopic biopsy with histology, H. pylori testing (rapid urease test, urea breath test, stool antigen).
167:
Burning epigastric pain relieved by food in a 16-year-old girl most probably indicates duodenal ulcer (peptic ulcer disease), and the commonest aetiological agent is Helicobacter pylori.

Duodenal ulcer pain is typically relieved by food and recurs 2–3 hours after meals and at night, because food neutralises acid. H. pylori is present in nearly all patients with duodenal ulcers; it causes antral gastritis with increased gastrin and acid secretion and duodenal gastric metaplasia, on which the bacteria colonise.

Other causes are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumour), and smoking and stress as co-factors. The ulcer is usually in the first part of the duodenum, is punched-out, and is almost never malignant. Diagnosis is by endoscopy and testing for H. pylori (urease test, urea breath test, stool antigen, histology); treatment is by eradication therapy (proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics).
168:
Relapsing bloody diarrhoea with lower abdominal pain in a young adult is most commonly due to inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) or infective colitis (shigellosis, amoebiasis, and others); less often Crohn disease, ischaemic colitis or colorectal polyps and carcinoma.

Common causes

  • Inflammatory: ulcerative colitis (most likely in a 25-year-old with a relapsing course), Crohn colitis.
  • Infective: bacillary dysentery (Shigella, Campylobacter, enteroinvasive E. coli), amoebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica), Salmonella, and tuberculosis.
  • Others: ischaemic colitis, haemorrhoids, colonic polyps and carcinoma.

Diagnosis

  1. Stool examination: microscopy for ova, cysts and trophozoites, pus cells and red cells; culture; stool occult blood.
  2. Blood: complete blood count, ESR, CRP, and serology.
  3. Colonoscopy with multiple biopsies and histopathology: in ulcerative colitis, there is continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and branching, and pseudopolyps, with no granulomas.
  4. Imaging (barium enema, CT) when needed.
170:
For a polypoid growth in the caecum, the specimens that can be sent are colonoscopic biopsy of the lesion and, if surgery is done, the resected segment (right hemicolectomy), along with regional lymph nodes and blood tests for tumour markers.

Specimens

  1. Endoscopic (colonoscopic) biopsy taken from the growth (multiple bites), for histopathological diagnosis (adenoma versus adenocarcinoma).
  2. Polypectomy specimen if the polyp is small and pedunculated; the whole specimen is submitted with the stalk margin inked.
  3. Resected specimen (right hemicolectomy) with proximal and distal margins, mesentery and regional lymph nodes, for diagnosis, grading and staging.
  4. Cytology (brush) and FNAC of liver deposits or enlarged nodes.
  5. Blood: CEA as a tumour marker (for monitoring), and haemoglobin and iron studies (iron-deficiency anaemia from occult bleeding); stool occult blood.
172:
Lower abdominal pain and altered bowel habit with multiple space-occupying lesions in the liver most probably indicate colorectal adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases.

The liver is the commonest site for metastases from colorectal cancer, by spread through the portal vein. The lesions are multiple, firm, white nodules, often with central umbilication and necrosis.

How to proceed in the laboratory

  1. Histopathology: FNAC or ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the liver lesion (metastatic adenocarcinoma with glandular pattern), and colonoscopic biopsy of the primary tumour.
  2. Blood tests: complete blood count (anaemia), liver function tests (raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT), and serum CEA (raised).
  3. Stool examination for occult blood.
  4. Immunohistochemistry (CK20 positive, CK7 negative, CDX2 positive) to support colonic origin, and mismatch repair and RAS/BRAF testing.
  5. Imaging: CT scan, ultrasound and colonoscopy for the primary lesion and for staging.
188:
A right hemicolectomy specimen with an ulcerated lesion encircling the lumen, with a variegated cut surface, is most likely adenocarcinoma of the colon (annular, ulcerative type).

Gross features: right-sided colon cancers are usually polypoid or fungating exophytic masses; left-sided are annular, constricting ("napkin-ring") ulcerated lesions. The cut surface is variegated grey-white, with haemorrhage, necrosis and mucin.

Histopathology

  • Malignant glands lined by tall columnar cells with hyperchromatic, elongated, pseudostratified nuclei, with a "dirty" necrotic luminal debris.
  • The tumour is graded as well, moderately or poorly differentiated according to gland formation; mucinous (more than 50% extracellular mucin) and signet-ring types occur.
  • Desmoplastic stroma; invasion through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa and muscularis propria (invasion is what distinguishes carcinoma from adenoma with dysplasia).
  • Lymphovascular and perineural invasion, tumour deposits and regional lymph node metastases are reported, and staging is by TNM.
171:
Jaundice and fever after a recent blood transfusion most probably indicate acute viral hepatitis, transmitted by transfusion, most often hepatitis B (also hepatitis C).

Hepatitis B and C are blood-borne. After an incubation period (4–26 weeks for HBV), the patient develops a prodrome of malaise, anorexia and fever, followed by jaundice, dark urine and tender hepatomegaly, with markedly raised ALT and AST. Diagnosis is by HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, HBeAg and HBV DNA; for hepatitis C by anti-HCV and HCV RNA.

Complications

  1. Fulminant hepatitis (massive hepatic necrosis) with hepatic failure.
  2. Chronic hepatitis (more than 6 months) leading to cirrhosis.
  3. Carrier state (HBsAg positive).
  4. Hepatocellular carcinoma in chronic HBV and HCV infection.
  5. Extrahepatic: glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa and cryoglobulinaemia; co-infection with delta virus worsens the disease.
173:
Chronic alcohol abuse causes three main hepatic changes: hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis).

Changes in the liver

  1. Hepatic steatosis: large, soft, yellow, greasy liver; macrovesicular fatty change in hepatocytes; reversible with abstinence.
  2. Alcoholic hepatitis: hepatocyte swelling (ballooning) and necrosis, Mallory–Denk bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of cytokeratin), neutrophil infiltration, and perivenular and pericellular fibrosis (chicken-wire pattern).
  3. Alcoholic cirrhosis: the end stage; a shrunken liver with fine, uniform micronodules (less than 3 mm) that later become mixed or macronodular, with diffuse fibrous septa.

Causes of death in end-stage alcoholic liver disease: hepatic failure (hepatic encephalopathy and coma), bleeding from ruptured oesophageal varices (portal hypertension), hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma, infections (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, sepsis), and coagulopathy.
174:
Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the tip of the right scapula in an obese woman with gallstones is acute (or chronic) cholecystitis due to cholelithiasis (calculous cholecystitis).

The patient fits the "fat, female, fertile, forty" profile; most gallstones are cholesterol stones. Pain (biliary colic) results from a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch; a positive Murphy sign and fever indicate cholecystitis.

Complications

  1. Empyema of the gallbladder, gangrene and perforation with pericholecystitis or peritonitis.
  2. Mucocele and hydrops of the gallbladder, and chronic cholecystitis with a fibrotic, thickened wall.
  3. Choledocholithiasis and obstructive jaundice; ascending cholangitis; liver abscess.
  4. Acute pancreatitis (stone at the ampulla of Vater).
  5. Cholecystoenteric fistula and gallstone ileus.
  6. Carcinoma of the gallbladder (long-standing stones), and porcelain gallbladder.
175:
A nephrectomy specimen is sent to the pathology laboratory to establish the diagnosis, type, grade and stage of the disease, and to guide further treatment and prognosis. A malignant renal tumour metastasises by direct extension, through the renal vein (haematogenous), and through lymphatics.

Reasons for sending the specimen

  1. To confirm the diagnosis and determine the histological type (e.g., clear cell, papillary or chromophobe renal cell carcinoma; urothelial carcinoma; Wilms tumour).
  2. To grade the tumour (ISUP/Fuhrman nuclear grade).
  3. To stage the tumour (TNM): size, invasion of perinephric fat, renal vein or inferior vena cava, adrenal gland, and lymph nodes.
  4. To assess surgical margins (ureter, vein, and capsule).
  5. To identify non-neoplastic disease in the remaining parenchyma (pyonephrosis, hydronephrosis, chronic pyelonephritis, renal stones) and to guide prognosis and adjuvant therapy.

Metastasis of renal cell carcinoma

  • Direct extension: into the renal vein and inferior vena cava as a "tumour thrombus", and into the perinephric fat.
  • Haematogenous: to the lungs (commonest), bone, liver, brain and adrenals.
  • Lymphatic: to the hilar and para-aortic nodes.
176:
Prostatic chips from TURP most commonly show benign prostatic hyperplasia (nodular hyperplasia), and the differential diagnoses include prostatic carcinoma, prostatitis and, less commonly, other conditions.

Differential diagnosis

  1. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): nodules of glands and fibromuscular stroma; glands lined by two layers (inner columnar and outer basal cells), often with papillary infoldings and corpora amylacea.
  2. Prostatic adenocarcinoma: small, crowded glands lacking basal cells, with prominent nucleoli, perineural invasion; confirmed by absent basal cell markers (p63, high-molecular-weight keratin) and positive AMACR; graded by the Gleason/ISUP system. It is found incidentally in about 10% of TURP specimens.
  3. Chronic prostatitis: chronic inflammatory infiltrate; granulomatous prostatitis (post-TURP or BCG therapy).
  4. Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (high-grade PIN): a precursor lesion.
  5. Others: infarct, bladder neck urothelial carcinoma or urothelial carcinoma involving the prostate, and tuberculosis.
179:
The germ cell tumour that most commonly presents as a painless, heavy, gradually enlarging testicular mass is seminoma, the commonest testicular germ cell tumour, peaking at 30–40 years.

Gross: a large, homogeneous, soft, bulging, pale grey-white or cream, lobulated mass with a fleshy "fish-flesh" cut surface, usually well circumscribed, with little haemorrhage or necrosis; the tunica albuginea is usually intact.

Histomorphology

  • Sheets of uniform, large polygonal cells with distinct cell borders, abundant clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm (PAS positive), and a large central round nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli.
  • The cells are divided into lobules by delicate fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes (T-cells); there may be granulomas and syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells.
  • Immunohistochemistry: positive for OCT3/4, PLAP, c-KIT (CD117) and SALL4; negative for AFP.
  • It arises from germ cell neoplasia in situ, is very sensitive to radiotherapy and chemotherapy, and has an excellent prognosis. Serum hCG may be mildly raised, AFP is normal.
177: Invasive cervical (squamous cell) carcinoma caused by high-risk HPV (16, 18).
178:
The differential diagnoses of a curettage specimen with four months of vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain are endometrial carcinoma or atypical hyperplasia, endometrial hyperplasia, chronic endometritis, endometrial polyp, submucosal leiomyoma or adenomyosis, and retained products of conception.

  • Endometrial carcinoma or atypical hyperplasia
  • Endometrial hyperplasia (anovulatory oestrogen excess)
  • Chronic endometritis (plasma cells; PID, retained products, IUCD)
  • Endometrial polyp
  • Submucosal leiomyoma or adenomyosis (pelvic pain, menorrhagia)
  • Pregnancy complications (retained products, molar disease)
180: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst). Benign teratomas make up most germ cell tumours. Histology: see Q1284. Immature teratoma and dysgerminoma are the main malignant considerations in children and young women.
181: Fibroadenoma (see Q1302): rubbery, grey-white, well circumscribed, with biphasic intracanalicular or pericanalicular histology.
182:
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (skin involvement suggests locally advanced disease).

Histology

  • Nests, cords and tongues of malignant duct-type cells infiltrating the stroma.
  • Exuberant desmoplastic stroma.
  • Nottingham grade from tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitoses: grade 1 has tubules and small uniform nuclei; grade 3 has ragged sheets, enlarged irregular nuclei and necrosis.
  • Associated DCIS is common; lymphovascular invasion may be seen.
  • Report ER, PR and HER2.
183:
An ulcerated lesion over the lower leg of an elderly patient with foul-smelling discharge indicates squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, which commonly arises in a chronic ulcer or scar (Marjolin ulcer); basal cell carcinoma and malignant melanoma are the other considerations.

Predisposing factors include chronic venous ulcers, sinuses, burn scars, osteomyelitis and chronic irritation. It appears as an ulcer with raised, everted, indurated margins, which is invasive and slow to metastasise.

Metastasis: mainly by lymphatics to the regional (inguinal and popliteal) lymph nodes, and later through the blood to the lungs, liver and bone. Spread to nodes is the main route; distant metastasis is late. Histology shows nests and cords of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, and invasion of the dermis. Diagnosis is by biopsy from the edge of the ulcer.
184:
A discharging sinus over the tibia for 4 months, with a curettage specimen, most probably indicates chronic osteomyelitis (pyogenic, or tuberculous if there is caseation).

Points in favour

  1. Clinical: long-standing discharging sinus (draining pus and sometimes bone fragments), localised pain and swelling, history of previous acute osteomyelitis or trauma; the shin (tibia) is a common site.
  2. Radiology: a sequestrum (dead, dense bone fragment), surrounded by an involucrum (new reactive bone), and a Brodie abscess.
  3. Histology of curettage: necrotic bone (sequestrum), chronic inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages, with fibrosis and granulation tissue and reactive new bone formation.
  4. Laboratory: raised ESR and CRP, neutrophilia, and culture of discharge (Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism).
  5. In tuberculosis, caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells and acid-fast bacilli would be seen.

Complications: pathological fracture, amyloidosis, and squamous cell carcinoma in the sinus tract.
185:
A bone-forming mass in the upper tibia of a 12-year-old boy with a sun-ray (sunburst) appearance on X-ray is osteosarcoma (osteogenic sarcoma), the commonest primary malignant bone tumour in children and adolescents, which arises in the metaphysis around the knee.

Radiology: a destructive mass with a "sunburst" pattern of periosteal new bone and Codman triangle (periosteal elevation).

Histopathology

  • Malignant, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic spindle and polygonal cells (osteoblast-like) with atypical mitoses.
  • The diagnostic feature is the production of neoplastic osteoid (and bone) directly by the tumour cells, as irregular lace-like pink trabeculae; cartilage and fibrous areas may also be present.
  • Subtypes: osteoblastic, chondroblastic and fibroblastic.
  • Gross: a large, gritty, tan-white, haemorrhagic and necrotic mass in the metaphysis, breaking through the cortex into soft tissue.
  • It is associated with RB and TP53 mutations, Paget disease and previous radiation; it metastasises through blood, mainly to the lungs.
186:
A soft, subcutaneous swelling of mature adipocytes is a lipoma, the commonest benign soft tissue tumour; its malignant counterpart is liposarcoma.

Lipoma: a soft, mobile, well-encapsulated, yellow, lobulated mass of mature fat cells indistinguishable from normal fat, usually in the subcutaneous tissue of the trunk, neck and proximal limbs of adults; it rarely recurs after simple excision.

Liposarcoma: the malignant tumour of adipocytes, commonly in the deep soft tissue of the thigh and retroperitoneum in adults of 50–60 years. It has lipoblasts (cells with vacuolated cytoplasm and scalloped, indented hyperchromatic nuclei). Types: well-differentiated (with MDM2 and CDK4 amplification), myxoid (FUS–DDIT3 translocation), dedifferentiated and pleomorphic.
187:
Headache and vomiting for 3 days with a space-occupying lesion on CT in a 10-year-old boy suggest raised intracranial pressure, and the most probable lesion in this age group is a posterior fossa tumour, most commonly medulloblastoma (also pilocytic astrocytoma).

Medulloblastoma: a highly malignant, small round blue cell tumour of the cerebellum (midline vermis), with obstruction of the fourth ventricle causing hydrocephalus, headache, vomiting and ataxia. Histology shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, and Homer Wright rosettes; it is positive for synaptophysin.

Prognosis: it is aggressive and spreads through the CSF ("drop metastases") along the neuraxis. It is highly radiosensitive, and with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy the 5-year survival is about 70–80% (poor in group 3/MYC-amplified tumours). Pilocytic astrocytoma, by contrast, is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) tumour with Rosenthal fibres and an excellent prognosis after surgical removal.
189:
Recurrent, transient substernal chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest, in an obese middle-aged man is typical of stable (chronic) angina pectoris due to ischaemic heart disease, caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries.

Probable causes

  • Atherosclerotic stenosis of the coronary arteries (more than 70% narrowing) with a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. Risk factors: obesity, hypertension, diabetes, smoking and hyperlipidaemia.
  • Less commonly: coronary spasm (Prinzmetal angina), aortic stenosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
276:
Dysplasia literally means "disordered growth"; it is encountered principally in epithelial cells and is recognised by pleomorphism, large hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, architectural disarray with loss of orderly differentiation, and increased mitotic figures that are seen throughout the epithelium rather than confined to the basal layer.

Explanation

Dysplasia literally means "disordered growth". It is encountered principally in epithelial cells and is a premalignant alteration in which the cells show variable cytologic atypia and the epithelium shows architectural disarray with loss of orderly differentiation.

Features

  • Cells: considerable pleomorphism; large hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
  • Epithelium: in dysplastic squamous epithelium the normal progressive maturation from tall basal cells to flattened surface squames fails in part or entirely, with replacement by basal-like cells with hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Mitoses: increased in number and seen throughout the epithelium rather than only in the basal layer.
  • The lesion does not penetrate the basement membrane.

Significance

Dysplasia is a precursor of malignant transformation, but progression to cancer is not inevitable, and with removal of the inciting cause a dysplasia of moderate severity may be completely reversible. When dysplasia is severe and involves the full thickness of the epithelium it is called carcinoma in situ.
512:
Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels, which in tumours takes the form of neoangiogenesis, the sprouting of new vessels from pre-existing capillaries; it is essential for tumour growth beyond 1 to 2 mm in diameter.

A solid tumour, even if it carries all the genetic aberrations required for malignant transformation, cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it can induce a blood supply, since this distance is the maximum across which oxygen, nutrients and waste products can diffuse from existing vessels. Early in their development most tumours do not induce angiogenesis and remain small or in situ, possibly for years, until an "angiogenic switch" terminates this stage of quiescence.

Angiogenesis is controlled by a balance between angiogenesis promoters and inhibitors, and in tumours this balance is tilted in favour of the promoters. Angiogenesis is therefore an essential requirement for malignancy.

Angiogenesis is also critical in healing at sites of injury and in the development of collateral circulation at sites of ischaemia.

Steps. In tissue repair angiogenesis occurs mainly by sprouting:

  1. Vasodilation in response to nitric oxide and increased permeability induced by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
  2. Separation of pericytes from the abluminal surface and breakdown of the basement membrane by matrix metalloproteinases to allow formation of a vessel sprout.
  3. Migration of endothelial cells toward the area of tissue injury.
  4. Proliferation of endothelial cells just behind the leading "tip" cell.
  5. Remodelling into capillary tubes.
  6. Recruitment of periendothelial cells (pericytes for small capillaries, smooth muscle cells for larger vessels) to form the mature vessel.
  7. Suppression of endothelial proliferation and migration and deposition of the basement membrane.

Mediators. VEGF-A (mainly) stimulates endothelial migration and proliferation, the "angiogenic switch", promotes vasodilation through NO and helps form the lumen. FGF-2 stimulates endothelial proliferation and the migration of macrophages and fibroblasts. Angiopoietins 1 and 2 contribute to the structural maturation of vessels. PDGF recruits smooth muscle cells, and TGF-β suppresses endothelial proliferation and enhances ECM production, thereby stabilising the vessel.

The Notch pathway regulates sprouting and branching so that new vessels are properly spaced. Matrix metalloproteinases degrade ECM to permit extension of the vessel, and integrin-ECM interactions provide scaffold.

Angiogenesis in tumours. Growing cancers stimulate neoangiogenesis, in which new vessels sprout from capillaries. A solid tumour cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it induces angiogenesis, and early in their development most tumours do not do so until an "angiogenic switch" occurs. Hypoxia stabilises HIF1α, which activates the transcription of VEGF and bFGF. Tumour vessels are leaky, dilated and haphazardly connected, and angiogenesis also contributes to metastasis.
449:
Metabolic alkalosis is an acid–base disorder in which a primary rise in plasma bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ above 28 mmol/L) raises the blood pH above 7.45, caused by loss of acid or gain of alkali, and compensated by hypoventilation.

Compensation. Hypoventilation raises PCO₂; this is limited by hypoxia, so compensation is incomplete. The kidney normally excretes excess bicarbonate, so metabolic alkalosis persists only when renal bicarbonate excretion is impaired, as in volume depletion, chloride depletion and potassium depletion.

Classification and causes

  • Chloride-responsive (urine chloride low): vomiting, nasogastric suction, gastric outlet obstruction, diuretic therapy.
  • Chloride-resistant (urine chloride high): primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, severe potassium depletion.
  • Alkali gain: excess bicarbonate or antacid intake.

The arterial blood gas shows a high pH, high HCO₃⁻ (above 28 mmol/L) and compensatory rise in PCO₂. Alkalosis reduces the ionised calcium by increasing its binding to albumin, causing tetany, paraesthesias, muscle cramps and seizures; it also causes hypokalaemia (potassium shifts into cells and is lost in urine), hypoventilation, confusion, arrhythmias and, if severe, coma. It is maintained by volume depletion, chloride depletion and hypokalaemia, and is classified as chloride-responsive (urine chloride low) or chloride-resistant (urine chloride high).
1372:
Metabolic alkalosis is an acid–base disorder in which the primary abnormality is a rise in plasma bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ above 28 mmol/L) with a rise in blood pH above 7.45. It results from loss of non-volatile acid (H⁺) from the body or from gain of bicarbonate or other alkali.

Compensation. Hypoventilation raises PCO₂; this is limited by hypoxia, so compensation is incomplete. The kidney normally excretes excess bicarbonate, so metabolic alkalosis persists only when renal bicarbonate excretion is impaired, as in volume depletion, chloride depletion and potassium depletion.

Classification and causes

  • Chloride-responsive (urine chloride low): vomiting, nasogastric suction, gastric outlet obstruction, diuretic therapy.
  • Chloride-resistant (urine chloride high): primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, severe potassium depletion.
  • Alkali gain: excess bicarbonate or antacid intake.
209:
Squamous metaplasia is the replacement of another epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium. It is the most common epithelial metaplasia (columnar to squamous; Fig. 2.28). Examples:

  1. Respiratory tract in smokers: the normal ciliated columnar epithelial cells of the trachea and bronchi are replaced by stratified squamous epithelium in response to chronic irritation.
  2. Vitamin A (retinoic acid) deficiency: squamous metaplasia of the respiratory epithelium and of the cornea, the latter with highly deleterious effects on vision.
  3. Stones in the excretory ducts of the salivary glands: the normally secretory columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia from irritation and pressure.
  4. Stones in the pancreatic or bile ducts: the same mechanism.
210:
The metaplasia in Barrett oesophagus is epithelial metaplasia of the squamous to columnar type. The normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-like columnar (glandular) cells under the influence of refluxed gastric acid (chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux).

  • Cancers arising here are typically gland-forming adenocarcinomas.
  • Goblet cells identify intestinal metaplasia.
253:
Pathologic calcification is the abnormal tissue deposition of calcium salts, together with smaller amounts of iron, magnesium and other mineral salts. There are two forms.

1. Dystrophic calcification. Deposition occurs locally in dying or dead tissue, despite normal serum calcium and in the absence of any derangement in calcium metabolism.

  • Sites: areas of coagulative, caseous or liquefactive necrosis, foci of enzymatic fat necrosis, the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis, and aging or damaged heart valves (Fig. 2.34), e.g. calcific aortic stenosis. A tuberculous lymph node may be virtually converted to stone.
  • Morphology: fine white granules or clumps, gritty on cutting; with H&E the salts are basophilic, amorphous and granular, intracellular, extracellular or both. Heterotopic bone may form in the focus.

2. Metastatic calcification. Deposition in otherwise normal tissues, almost always due to hypercalcaemia from disturbed calcium metabolism. The four principal causes of hypercalcaemia are: (1) increased parathyroid hormone (hyperparathyroidism, or PTH-related protein from malignant tumours); (2) bone resorption (multiple myeloma, diffuse skeletal metastases, Paget disease, immobilisation); (3) vitamin D–related disorders (vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis); and (4) renal failure with phosphate retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
255:
Dystrophic calcification is the local deposition of calcium salts in dying (necrotic) or damaged tissue; it occurs despite normal serum calcium levels and in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism. In contrast, metastatic calcification affects normal tissues in hypercalcaemia.

  • Sites: areas of coagulative, caseous or liquefactive necrosis, foci of enzymatic fat necrosis, the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis, and aging or damaged heart valves (Fig. 2.34), e.g. calcific aortic stenosis. A tuberculous lymph node may be virtually converted to stone.
  • Morphology: fine white granules or clumps, gritty on cutting; with H&E the salts are basophilic, amorphous and granular, intracellular, extracellular or both. Heterotopic bone may form in the focus.
1279:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the main cause of carcinoma of the cervix. Nearly all precursor lesions and carcinomas involve one of about 15 high-risk types (mainly 16 and 18), whereas low-risk types (6, 11) cause condylomas and have weak E6/E7 activity.

Mechanism. The carcinogenic ability of HPV depends on the viral E6 and E7 proteins, which interfere with the tumour suppressor proteins p53 and RB, respectively.

  • Viral replication occurs in maturing squamous cells, which are normally arrested in G₁; HPV drives them through the cell cycle to use the host DNA synthesis machinery.
  • E7 promotes proteasomal degradation of RB and inhibits the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p21 and p27, enhancing cell cycle progression.
  • E6 promotes degradation of p53, impairing DNA-damage-induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
  • In most cancers the viral DNA is integrated into the host genome, which increases E6 and E7 expression and may dysregulate nearby oncogenes such as MYC; in precursor lesions and condylomas it is episomal.

HPV alone is not enough: only a few infected women develop cancer, so co-factors (smoking, immune compromise, multiparity, other infections) contribute. The nonavalent vaccine covers types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58 (see Q1278).
